name: The Fool
symbols: A youth steps toward a cliff edge, face lifted to the sky rather than the drop — the beginning made without calculating the fall.
A small white dog at his heels barks — instinct, the animal self that both warns and accompanies.
In one hand a white rose (purity of motive); over the shoulder a small bundle on a staff (the light baggage of one who travels unencumbered).
The sun rises behind him and mountains lie ahead — the known at his back, the unknown before him.

reading.upright: The Fool is the beginning that precedes knowledge: stepping into the unknown with openness rather than certainty. It favours first steps, spontaneity, and trust in one's own footing — the fall is real, but so is the ground.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Fool loses his balance: either the leap becomes heedless, taken without looking, or the edge becomes paralyzing and the step is never taken. It asks which of the two fears is at work.

elementalRegister.value: Air / Spirit (Major Arcana; yellow sky, feather in cap)
elementalRegister.note: The Fool is a Major Arcana card, so its element is spirit, but the yellow sky and the feather mark him as air: the element of breath, thought, and beginning. He moves through light rather than through solid ground.

numericalDegree.note: Zero is the unformed, the potential before any step is taken. It is the number of the open circle, not the closed one — a degree that precedes all degrees.

courtFunction.note: The Fool is not a court card; he is the archetype of the unformed self, prior to any social role.

figureType.value: A young human figure in motley, male or androgynous
figureType.note: The Fool is human but not yet individuated; his motley marks him as outside ordinary station, a traveller rather than a citizen.

posture.value: Standing, one foot lifted over a cliff edge, body leaning forward
posture.note: The posture is one of uncalculated forward motion: the step is being taken before the ground has been checked.

gesture.value: Right hand holds a white rose; left hand carries a bundle on a staff over the shoulder
gesture.note: The rose is the gesture of purity and love; the bundle is the gesture of light baggage — what is carried is not a burden but a willingness.

gaze.value: Face lifted upward, not looking at the cliff
gaze.note: The gaze is upward and outward, toward the sky rather than the drop. It is the gaze of trust, or of inattention, depending on how one reads it.

movementDirection.note: Rightward movement in the deck is the direction of the future and the conscious will; the Fool moves toward what is not yet known.

centralObject.value: A white rose and a bundle on a staff
centralObject.note: The rose is the soul's offering; the bundle is the traveller's minimal equipment. Neither is a weapon or a tool of control.

heldObject.value: White rose (right hand), staff with bundle (left hand)
heldObject.note: The rose is held lightly, as an emblem rather than a tool; the staff is carried over the shoulder, as a support rather than a weapon.

creature.value: A small white dog at his heels
creature.note: The dog is instinct, the animal self that both barks a warning and accompanies the step. It is not an enemy but a companion.

tool.value: A staff (not a wand or sword)
tool.note: The staff is the simplest tool, a walking stick rather than an instrument of power. It is support, not domination.

writtenWord.note: There is no text, no law, no map. The Fool is prior to the written word; his knowledge is not inscribed.

landscape.value: A high, bare mountain path ending at a cliff edge; a valley or abyss below
landscape.note: The landscape is the threshold between the known and the unknown. The cliff is not an obstacle but the place where the step must be taken.

architecture.note: There is no architecture, no city, no institution. The Fool is outside the built world.

threshold.value: The cliff edge is the threshold
threshold.note: The cliff edge is the literal threshold: the line between the ground that is known and the air that is not.

celestialBody.value: The sun, bright and yellow, behind him
celestialBody.note: The sun is the source of light and life, and its position behind the Fool suggests that the light is not something he is seeking but something he already carries.

weather.note: The weather is fair. The Fool is not stepping into a storm; the difficulty is not in the conditions but in the step itself.

symmetry.value: Asymmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is asymmetrical: the Fool leans forward, the dog is at his heels, the bundle is on one shoulder. The imbalance is the point — the Fool is not in equilibrium.

repetitionCount.value: One of each (one rose, one bundle, one dog)
repetitionCount.note: There is no repetition. The Fool is a singular figure in a singular moment.

verticalAxis.value: The sky above, the abyss below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the axis of the fall: the Fool is suspended between the sky he looks toward and the ground he has not yet left.

horizontalAxis.value: Left (the dog, the past) and right (the cliff, the future)
horizontalAxis.note: The dog at the left heel is the instinct that comes from behind; the cliff at the right is the future that has not yet been met.

inversion.value: No inversion of the figure; a partial inversion in the lifted foot
inversion.note: The Fool is upright, but his foot is lifted — a leaning out of the vertical, a partial inversion that marks the beginning of a fall or a flight.

clothing.value: Motley, colourful, with a feathered cap
clothing.note: The motley is the dress of the jester and the traveller: it marks him as outside ordinary rank, free from the constraints of station.

nudity.note: The Fool is not naked, but he is unarmoured. His clothing is light, not protective.

crown.value: A feathered cap, not a crown
crown.note: He wears no crown. The Fool has no authority, no rule, no claim to power.

wound.note: There is no wound, no injury. The Fool is not yet marked by experience.

binding.note: There are no chains, no bonds. The Fool is unbound, for better and for worse.

water.note: There is no water in the card. The Fool is not yet in the realm of feeling or the unconscious; he is in the air.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Fool's energy is air and light, not heat.

vegetation.value: Sparse; a few plants on the rocky path
vegetation.note: The vegetation is minimal, marking the altitude and the bareness of the threshold. This is not a garden.

stone.value: The rocky cliff and the mountain path
stone.note: Stone is the ground that is being left. It is hard, real, and about to be abandoned.

polarity.note: The Fool's remedy-pair is the World: the completion that the Fool's beginning is moving toward. The Fool is the first step; the World is the last.

remedy.note: The remedy is not to stop the step but to add attention to it: trust the ground, but also look at it.

prescribedAct.value: Take the first step before you feel ready, but check the ground beneath your foot.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the step itself, taken with a measure of awareness. The Fool's lesson is not recklessness but the courage to begin.

detailedReading: The Fool is the card of the beginning that precedes knowledge, and its detailed features show why the beginning is both a gift and a risk. Its elemental register is air and spirit: the yellow sky, the feather in the cap, and the lifted foot all mark a figure who is moving through breath and light rather than through solid ground. The numerical degree is zero — the unformed, the open circle — and the posture is the posture of the uncalculated step: one foot over the cliff edge, the gaze lifted to the sky rather than lowered to the drop. The white rose in one hand is the gesture of purity, the bundle on the staff the gesture of light baggage; neither is a tool of control. The small white dog at the heels is instinct, a companion rather than an enemy. The landscape is the threshold itself: a bare mountain path ending at a cliff, with no architecture, no written word, and no water — the Fool is outside the built world and outside the realm of feeling, in the element of air. The asymmetry of the composition, the absence of a crown, the absence of a wound, and the absence of binding all confirm that the Fool is unmarked and unbound. The prescribed act follows from this: take the first step before you feel ready, but check the ground beneath your foot. The remedy is trust with attention — the courage to begin, held together with the willingness to look.

name: The Magician
symbols: A figure raises a wand to the sky while pointing to the earth — will above, matter below, the channel between them made active.
The infinity symbol above his head — limitlessness of the potential being concentrated into a single act.
A table before him holds a cup, sword, coin and wand — all four elements of the world, gathered and available.
Roses and lilies in the garden behind him — desire and thought in bloom, the raw material of his work.

reading.upright: The Magician is the moment of concentrated will — everything needed is already on the table, and the task is to focus it. Skill, initiative, and the deliberate use of one's resources.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Magician's power is misused or dispersed: tricks instead of craft, manipulation instead of direction, or talent left on the table unused.

elementalRegister.value: Air / Spirit (Major Arcana; yellow sky, wand raised to sky)
elementalRegister.note: The Magician's element is spirit, but the yellow background and the raised wand mark him as an agent of air: the element of thought and communication, made active.

numericalDegree.note: One is the number of the single point, the beginning of manifestation. It is the degree at which potential becomes a direction.

courtFunction.note: The Magician is not a court card; he is the archetype of the will that organises the world.

figureType.value: A standing human figure in red robes
figureType.note: He is fully human, dressed in the red of active will. He is not a god but a human being who has learned to channel force.

posture.value: Standing upright, one arm raised, one arm lowered
posture.note: The upright posture is the posture of authority; the raised and lowered arms form a vertical channel between above and below.

gesture.value: Right hand raises a wand to the sky; left hand points to the earth
gesture.note: This is the classic gesture of 'as above, so below': the will is connected to both the celestial and the material, and the Magician is the conduit.

gaze.value: Facing forward, toward the viewer
gaze.note: The gaze is direct and unflinching: the Magician is addressing the world, not avoiding it.

movementDirection.value: Static (standing), but the gesture implies a downward flow
movementDirection.note: The movement is not across the ground but along the vertical axis: force is being drawn down from the sky and directed into the earth.

centralObject.value: A wand raised to the sky and a table of four elemental tools
centralObject.note: The wand is the channel of will; the table is the set of resources — cup, sword, coin, wand — that the will can organise.

heldObject.value: A wand in the right hand; the left hand points downward
heldObject.note: The wand is not a weapon but an instrument of direction; the pointing hand is the gesture of channeling, not grasping.

creature.note: There is no creature in the Magician's card. The animal instincts are not present; this is a card of conscious, human will.

tool.value: Wand, cup, sword, and pentacle on the table
tool.note: All four suits are present as tools. The Magician has access to every element, and the task is to use them in right proportion.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Magician's knowledge is not inscribed in a book but enacted in gesture.

landscape.value: A garden with roses and lilies
landscape.note: The garden is the cultivated world, the raw material of nature brought into order by human care.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Magician works in the open, on the materials themselves, not within an institution.

threshold.note: There is no threshold. The Magician is not crossing from one state to another; he is operating at the point where will meets matter.

celestialBody.value: The sun, implied by the bright yellow sky
celestialBody.note: The light is overhead and full, suggesting that the Magician's work is done in the clear light of consciousness.

weather.note: The weather is fair. There is no storm; the difficulty is not in the conditions but in the concentration of will.

symmetry.value: Asymmetrical (one arm up, one down), but balanced
symmetry.note: The composition is asymmetrical in gesture but balanced in force: the up and down are held in a single vertical line.

repetitionCount.note: The four tools are the complete set of elements. The number four is the number of the material world, organised and complete.

verticalAxis.value: The raised wand above, the pointing hand below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the channel of the card: the Magician is the point at which the above and the below are connected.

horizontalAxis.value: The table of tools in front of him
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the plane of the material: the tools are laid out before him, available to be used.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Magician is fully upright, his gestures clear and deliberate.

clothing.value: Red robes with a white undergarment
clothing.note: Red is the colour of active will; white is purity of intention. The clothing marks him as a deliberate agent, not a passive one.

nudity.note: The Magician is fully clothed. His power is mediated by intention and form, not exposed.

crown.value: The infinity symbol above his head (not a crown)
crown.note: He wears no crown, but the infinity symbol is the mark of limitless potential. His authority is not social but cosmic.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Magician is not suffering; he is acting.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Magician is free to use his tools.

water.value: Absent (the cup is a tool, not a landscape)
water.note: Water is present only as one of the four tools. The Magician is not immersed in feeling; he handles it.

fire.value: Absent (the wand is a tool, not a flame)
fire.note: Fire is present only as the wand. The Magician directs heat; he is not consumed by it.

vegetation.value: Roses and lilies in the garden
vegetation.note: Roses are desire, lilies are thought. Both are cultivated, both are in bloom: the Magician's raw material is alive and available.

stone.value: Absent (the table may be stone, but it is not the subject)
stone.note: Stone is not a feature of the card. The Magician works with living materials, not with the dead weight of the ground.

polarity.note: The Magician's remedy-pair is the High Priestess: he is active will, she is receptive intuition. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Magician's active will is the Priestess's stillness: sometimes the right use of power is to wait and listen.

prescribedAct.value: Choose one tool and use it deliberately today, rather than trying to use all four at once.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the concentration of will into a single, deliberate gesture. The Magician's lesson is not that everything is possible, but that one thing can be done now.

detailedReading: The Magician is the card of concentrated will, and its detailed features show how that will is organised. Its elemental register is air and spirit: the yellow sky, the raised wand, and the direct gaze all mark a figure who is working in the clear light of consciousness. The numerical degree is one — the single point, the beginning of manifestation — and the posture is the upright posture of authority, with one arm raised to the sky and one pointing to the earth. This is the gesture of 'as above, so below': the will is connected to both the celestial and the material, and the Magician is the conduit between them. The table before him holds the four tools of the suits — cup, sword, coin, and wand — which means that all four elements are available; the task is to use them in right proportion. The garden of roses and lilies behind him is the cultivated raw material of desire and thought, alive and in bloom. There is no architecture, no written word, no threshold, and no creature: the Magician is not inside an institution, not following a text, not crossing a boundary, and not driven by instinct. The asymmetry of the gesture is balanced by the vertical axis of force. The prescribed act follows from this: choose one tool and use it deliberately today, rather than trying to use all four at once. The remedy is receptivity — the High Priestess's stillness — because the active will needs to be corrected by the capacity to wait and listen.

name: The High Priestess
symbols: She sits between a black pillar and a white one — the two poles of experience, held in balance rather than resolved.
A crescent moon at her feet — the subconscious, the tide, the reflected light of what is not yet known.
Behind her a veil of pomegranates — the fruit of Persephone, marking the threshold to the underworld of the hidden.
A scroll marked TORA rests half-hidden in her lap — esoteric law, given only to those who look.

reading.upright: The High Priestess is the knowledge that arrives before explanation — intuition, dreams, the quiet sense of what is true. She asks for stillness and attention rather than action.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Priestess is either secreting what should be shared, or the querent is ignoring the inner voice in favour of the surface story.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; blue robes, crescent moon, water behind the veil)
elementalRegister.note: The High Priestess is a Major Arcana card, but her imagery is dominated by water: the blue robes, the crescent moon, and the water behind the veil mark her as the card of the unconscious and the receptive.

numericalDegree.note: Two is the number of polarity and reflection. The Priestess is the second point, the mirror that receives the light of the first.

courtFunction.note: The High Priestess is not a court card; she is the archetype of the inner knower, not a social role.

figureType.value: A seated human woman in blue robes
figureType.note: She is human but hieratic, seated rather than standing. Her posture marks her as a guardian of knowledge rather than an agent of action.

posture.value: Seated, upright, between two pillars
posture.note: The seated posture is the posture of stability and contemplation; she is not moving, because the knowledge she holds is not arrived at by movement.

gesture.value: Hands resting on the scroll in her lap; one hand slightly open
gesture.note: The gesture is one of holding and concealing: the scroll is present but not displayed, available only to the one who looks closely.

gaze.value: Facing forward, but the eyes are veiled or half-closed
gaze.note: The gaze is inward rather than outward. She is looking at what is not visible to the ordinary eye.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Priestess is the point of stillness in which the hidden becomes available.

centralObject.value: The scroll marked TORA, half-hidden in her lap
centralObject.note: The scroll is the esoteric law, the hidden teaching. It is not a book for everyone; it is given only to those who look.

heldObject.note: She holds the scroll lightly, not displaying it. The holding is an act of guardianship, not of possession.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Priestess's knowledge is not instinctual; it is intuitive, which is a different order.

tool.value: The scroll (a text, not a weapon or instrument)
tool.note: Her only tool is the written word, but it is a hidden word. The tool is knowledge itself.

writtenWord.note: The written word is present, but it is partially concealed. The Priestess is the guardian of the text, not its public reader.

landscape.value: A temple interior with a veil behind her
landscape.note: The landscape is an interior, a sacred enclosure. The Priestess is not in the open world; she is in the place where the hidden is kept.

architecture.value: Two pillars (black and white) and a veil
architecture.note: The pillars are the architecture of polarity: the black and white, the known and unknown, held in balance. The veil is the boundary between the visible and the hidden.

threshold.value: The veil of pomegranates behind her
threshold.note: The veil is the threshold. The pomegranates mark it as the threshold to the underworld, the realm of the hidden and the dead.

celestialBody.value: The crescent moon at her feet
celestialBody.note: The moon is the celestial body of the unconscious, the reflected light that illuminates what the sun cannot reach.

weather.note: There is no weather. The Priestess is in an interior space, protected from the elements, where the only climate is the climate of the mind.

symmetry.value: Balanced and symmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the two pillars, the seated figure, the veil. The symmetry is the point — the Priestess holds the opposites in balance.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of polarity. The two pillars are the structural expression of the card's balance.

verticalAxis.value: The pillars rise above and below; the moon is at the feet
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the moon at the feet) to the architectural (the pillars). The Priestess is the point of connection.

horizontalAxis.value: The veil behind her, the scroll in front
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of concealment and revelation: what is behind the veil and what is held in the lap.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Priestess is upright, seated, and still.

clothing.value: Blue robes, with a crescent crown
clothing.note: Blue is the colour of water and receptivity; the crown is the mark of her authority, but it is a lunar crown, not a solar one.

nudity.note: The Priestess is fully clothed. Her knowledge is veiled, not exposed.

crown.value: A crown of the crescent moon
crown.note: The crown is the mark of her authority, but it is the authority of the moon, not the sun: the authority of reflection and intuition.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Priestess is not marked by suffering; she is marked by knowledge.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Priestess is free, but her freedom is the freedom of stillness, not of movement.

water.value: Water is implied behind the veil (the realm of the unconscious)
water.note: Water is not visible, but it is present behind the veil. The Priestess is the guardian of the unconscious, the deep water that is not shown.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Priestess's element is water, not fire.

vegetation.value: Pomegranates and palms on the veil
vegetation.note: The pomegranates are the fruit of the underworld; the palms are the mark of the sacred. The vegetation is symbolic, not natural.

stone.note: The stone pillars are the architecture of permanence. The Priestess's knowledge is not transient; it is built.

polarity.note: The High Priestess's remedy-pair is the Magician: she is receptive intuition, he is active will. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Priestess's stillness is the Magician's deliberate act: sometimes the hidden knowledge must be brought into the world through a gesture.

prescribedAct.value: Sit with the question without answering it today; let the answer arrive in its own time.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of waiting. The Priestess's lesson is that not all knowledge is arrived at by seeking; some of it is arrived at by listening.

detailedReading: The High Priestess is the card of the knowledge that arrives before explanation, and its detailed features show how that knowledge is guarded. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the blue robes, the crescent moon, and the water implied behind the veil mark her as the card of the unconscious and the receptive. The numerical degree is two — the number of polarity and reflection — and the posture is seated and still, between two pillars, one black and one white. The pillars are the architecture of polarity: the known and the unknown held in balance. The gesture is one of holding and concealing: the scroll marked TORA rests half-hidden in her lap, available only to the one who looks closely. The gaze is inward, veiled; she is looking at what is not visible to the ordinary eye. The veil of pomegranates behind her is the threshold to the underworld, the realm of the hidden. The crescent moon at her feet is the celestial body of the unconscious. There is no creature, no fire, no wound, and no binding: the Priestess is not driven by instinct, not consumed by heat, not marked by suffering, and not restrained. The symmetry of the composition confirms that she is the point of balance. The prescribed act follows from this: sit with the question without answering it today; let the answer arrive in its own time. The remedy is action — the Magician's deliberate gesture — because the receptive knowledge needs to be corrected by the capacity to act.

name: The Empress
symbols: She reclines on cushions in an open field — ease, sensuality, the body at rest in the world.
A field of ripe wheat lies before her — harvest, fertility, the reward of nature's slow work.
A crown of twelve stars — cosmic order, the whole zodiac gathered on a single head.
A heart-shaped shield marked with the sign of Venus — love and creativity as her domain.

reading.upright: The Empress is abundance that arrives through the body and the natural world: fertility, generosity, beauty, and the slow ripening of what has been tended.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Empress's abundance is blocked or distorted — creativity stalled, nurture turned into smothering, or self-neglect mistaken for modesty.

elementalRegister.value: Earth / Spirit (Major Arcana; green robes, wheat field, garden)
elementalRegister.note: The Empress is a Major Arcana card, but her imagery is dominated by earth: the green robes, the wheat, and the garden mark her as the card of material abundance and natural fertility.

numericalDegree.note: Three is the number of creation and fruition. The Empress is the third point, the moment at which the seed becomes the harvest.

courtFunction.note: The Empress is not a court card; she is the archetype of the nurturing, creative principle.

figureType.value: A seated human woman, pregnant or reclining, in a garden
figureType.note: She is human and bodily, seated in ease. Her pregnancy or reclining posture marks her as the figure of fertility and reception.

posture.value: Seated or reclining on cushions, at ease
posture.note: The posture is one of comfort and openness. The Empress is not striving; she is receiving and generating.

gesture.value: One hand may hold a sceptre; the other rests open
gesture.note: The sceptre is the mark of authority, but it is held loosely. The open hand is the gesture of generosity.

gaze.value: Facing forward or slightly downward, toward the world
gaze.note: The gaze is outward and benevolent. The Empress is looking at the world she nurtures.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Empress's power is in growth, not in motion.

centralObject.value: The wheat field before her and the shield of Venus
centralObject.note: The wheat is the harvest, the reward of slow growth; the shield is the mark of love and beauty as her domain.

heldObject.note: The sceptre is the tool of rule, but it is not raised or brandished. The Empress's authority is natural, not imposed.

creature.value: Absent (though the natural world is present)
creature.note: There is no single creature. The Empress's world is the whole of nature, not a particular animal.

tool.value: The sceptre (a symbol of rule, not a weapon)
tool.note: Her tool is the sceptre, but it is a sceptre of fertility, not of war.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Empress's law is written in the body and the natural world, not in a book.

landscape.value: A lush garden with a wheat field and a waterfall
landscape.note: The landscape is the garden, the cultivated earth. It is abundant, fertile, and at rest.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Empress is in the open field, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: There is no threshold. The Empress is not crossing from one state to another; she is at the centre of her domain.

celestialBody.note: The stars are the celestial order, the zodiac gathered on her head. The Empress is the point at which the cosmic and the earthly meet.

weather.note: The weather is fair and fertile. There is no storm; the climate is one of growth.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the reclining figure is central, the garden surrounds)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced but not rigid. The symmetry is the symmetry of the natural world, not of architecture.

repetitionCount.note: The number twelve is the number of the zodiac, the complete cycle of the heavens.

verticalAxis.value: The crown of stars above, the wheat below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the cosmic (the stars) to the earthly (the wheat). The Empress is the point of connection between heaven and earth.

horizontalAxis.value: The garden extends to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the plane of the natural world, abundant and open.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Empress is upright and at ease.

clothing.value: Green robes, loose and flowing
clothing.note: Green is the colour of vegetation and growth. The loose robes mark her as a figure of ease, not of constraint.

nudity.value: Absent (she is clothed, but the robes are loose)
nudity.note: The Empress is not nude, but her clothing is not restrictive. Her body is present but not exposed.

crown.note: The crown is the mark of her cosmic authority. It is a crown of stars, not of metal — her rule is natural, not political.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Empress is not suffering; she is in the fullness of her power.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Empress is free, and her freedom is the freedom of the natural world.

water.note: Water is present as a waterfall, the flow of life and fertility. It is not the deep water of the unconscious but the fresh water of growth.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Empress's element is earth, not fire.

vegetation.value: Wheat, trees, and a lush garden
vegetation.note: Vegetation is the dominant feature of the card. The Empress is the card of the harvest, the reward of growth.

stone.value: Absent (the shield is the only hard object)
stone.note: Stone is not a feature of the card. The Empress's world is soft and fertile, not hard and unyielding.

polarity.note: The Empress's remedy-pair is the Emperor: she is nurture, he is structure. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Empress's abundance is the Emperor's structure: sometimes nurture needs a boundary to be fruitful.

prescribedAct.value: Tend one living thing today — a plant, a person, a project — and let it grow at its own pace.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of nurture. The Empress's lesson is that abundance is not seized but cultivated.

detailedReading: The Empress is the card of abundance that arrives through the body and the natural world, and its detailed features show how that abundance is cultivated. Its elemental register is earth and spirit: the green robes, the wheat field, and the garden mark her as the card of material fertility. The numerical degree is three — the number of creation and fruition — and the posture is seated or reclining, at ease. The gesture is one of holding and openness: the sceptre is held lightly, the hand is open. The gaze is outward and benevolent, toward the world she nurtures. The central objects are the wheat field and the shield of Venus: the harvest and the mark of love. The landscape is a lush garden with a waterfall, and the crown of twelve stars connects the cosmic to the earthly. There is no architecture, no threshold, no creature, no fire, and no wound: the Empress is in the open field of nature, not in a city or a temple, not crossing a boundary, not driven by instinct, not consumed by heat, and not marked by suffering. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the natural world. The prescribed act follows from this: tend one living thing today and let it grow at its own pace. The remedy is structure — the Emperor's boundary — because abundance needs form to be fruitful.

name: The Emperor
symbols: He sits on a stone throne carved with rams' heads — Aries, the sign of initiative, marking authority that has been earned.
He holds an ankh scepter in one hand and a globe in the other — life and dominion, held together.
Armor shows beneath his red robe — power that is ready, even when at rest.
Bare mountains rise behind him — the stark, unyielding ground on which order is built.

reading.upright: The Emperor is structure, law, and the protective authority that makes a life possible. He represents the father-principle: boundaries, responsibility, and the decision to take charge.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Emperor becomes domination, rigidity, or the absence of a spine — either too much control or none at all.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; red robes, ram heads, bare mountains)
elementalRegister.note: The Emperor is a Major Arcana card, but his imagery is dominated by fire: the red robes, the ram heads of Aries, and the bare mountains mark him as the card of active, initiating will.

numericalDegree.note: Four is the number of structure and stability. The Emperor is the fourth point, the moment at which the world is organised into a form.

courtFunction.note: The Emperor is not a court card; he is the archetype of the structuring, authoritative principle.

figureType.value: A seated human man in armour and red robes
figureType.note: He is human and armoured, seated on a throne. His armour marks him as a figure of war and protection, not of ease.

posture.value: Seated upright on a stone throne, facing forward
posture.note: The upright posture is the posture of authority. The Emperor is not leaning; he is established.

gesture.value: Right hand holds an ankh sceptre; left hand holds a globe
gesture.note: The ankh is life, the globe is dominion. The gesture is one of holding both together: authority over life and over the world.

gaze.value: Facing forward, direct and unflinching
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of command. The Emperor is looking at the world he rules.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Emperor's power is in stability, not in motion.

centralObject.value: The ankh sceptre and the globe
centralObject.note: The sceptre is the tool of rule; the globe is the object of rule. Together they are the symbols of authority over life and over the world.

heldObject.note: The held objects are the instruments of rule. They are held firmly, not lightly.

creature.value: Ram heads carved on the throne
creature.note: The rams are the sign of Aries, the initiating fire. They are carved into the throne, marking the Emperor's authority as earned through initiative.

tool.note: The sceptre is the tool of command. It is a rod of authority, not a weapon of war.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Emperor's law is not written in a book; it is written in the structure of the world.

landscape.value: Bare mountains behind the throne
landscape.note: The landscape is stark and unyielding. The mountains are the ground on which order is built, but they are not fertile; they are the ground of necessity.

architecture.note: The throne is the architecture of rule. It is stone, permanent, and carved with the signs of authority.

threshold.note: There is no threshold. The Emperor is established in his domain, not crossing into another.

celestialBody.value: Absent (the light is implied but not shown)
celestialBody.note: There is no celestial body. The Emperor's authority is not derived from the heavens; it is established on the earth.

weather.note: The weather is clear but not warm. The climate is one of necessity, not of ease.

symmetry.value: Balanced and symmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the seated figure, the throne, the mountains. The symmetry is the point — the Emperor is the centre of order.

repetitionCount.value: Four rams' heads on the throne
repetitionCount.note: The number four is the number of structure. The four rams mark the four corners of the Emperor's domain.

verticalAxis.value: The mountains rise behind him; the throne is on the ground
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the earthly throne to the mountain heights. The Emperor is the point at which the ground becomes the rule.

horizontalAxis.value: The sceptre and the globe are held to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of rule: the sceptre on one side, the globe on the other.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Emperor is upright and established.

clothing.value: Red robes over armour
clothing.note: Red is the colour of active will; the armour is the mark of readiness. The Emperor is dressed for both rule and war.

nudity.note: The Emperor is fully clothed and armoured. His power is mediated by form and protection.

crown.value: A crown (implied by the throne and the sceptre)
crown.note: The crown is the mark of his authority. It is a crown of rule, not of sanctity.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Emperor is not suffering; he is commanding.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Emperor is free to rule.

water.note: There is no water. The Emperor's element is fire and earth, not water.

fire.value: Absent (the red robes are the colour of fire, but there is no flame)
fire.note: Fire is present as colour, not as flame. The Emperor's heat is the heat of will, not of destruction.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Emperor's world is stark and unyielding, not fertile.

stone.value: The stone throne and the bare mountains
stone.note: Stone is the dominant material of the card. The Emperor's rule is built on stone, not on sand.

polarity.note: The Emperor's remedy-pair is the Empress: he is structure, she is nurture. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Emperor's rigidity is the Empress's nurture: sometimes structure needs to soften to be fruitful.

prescribedAct.value: Set one clear boundary today, and hold it without apology.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the establishment of structure. The Emperor's lesson is that authority is not domination; it is the making of a form within which life can flourish.

detailedReading: The Emperor is the card of structure and protective authority, and its detailed features show how that authority is established. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the red robes, the ram heads of Aries, and the bare mountains mark him as the card of active, initiating will. The numerical degree is four — the number of structure and stability — and the posture is seated upright on a stone throne, facing forward. The gesture is one of holding both life and dominion: the ankh sceptre in one hand, the globe in the other. The gaze is direct and unflinching, the gaze of command. The central objects are the sceptre and the globe, the instruments of rule. The landscape is stark and unyielding: bare mountains behind the throne, no vegetation, no water. The stone throne is carved with four rams' heads, marking the Emperor's authority as earned through initiative. There is no threshold, no celestial body, no creature, no wound, and no binding: the Emperor is established in his domain, not crossing a boundary, not derived from the heavens, not driven by instinct, not marked by suffering, and not restrained. The symmetry of the composition confirms that he is the centre of order. The prescribed act follows from this: set one clear boundary today, and hold it without apology. The remedy is nurture — the Empress's softness — because structure needs to be corrected by the capacity to nourish.

name: The Hierophant
symbols: He raises his right hand in blessing — the gesture of the one authorised to transmit.
A triple crown marks the three worlds of body, mind and spirit — hierarchy spanning all of them.
Two crossed keys lie at his feet — the keys to sacred knowledge, kept by the institution.
Two tonsured monks kneel before him — the faithful receiving the transmitted teaching.

reading.upright: The Hierophant is the institution and the inherited form: tradition, education, the shared belief that holds a community together. He asks what has been handed down.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Hierophant asks whether the inherited form still serves — a call to rebel against dogma, or to find one's own spiritual authority.

elementalRegister.value: Earth / Spirit (Major Arcana; seated between pillars, red and grey robes)
elementalRegister.note: The Hierophant is a Major Arcana card, but his imagery is dominated by earth: the seated posture, the institutional setting, and the red and grey robes mark him as the card of established tradition and transmitted form.

numericalDegree.note: Five is the number of the human figure, the point at which the cosmic order becomes a social order. The Hierophant is the fifth point, the teacher who transmits the law.

courtFunction.note: The Hierophant is not a court card; he is the archetype of the institution and the transmitted teaching.

figureType.value: A seated human man in papal robes, with two kneeling monks
figureType.note: He is human and institutional, seated in authority. The kneeling monks mark him as the transmitter of a teaching, not its originator.

posture.value: Seated on a throne, upright, between two pillars
posture.note: The seated posture is the posture of established authority. The Hierophant is not moving; he is transmitting.

gesture.value: Right hand raised in blessing; left hand holds a triple cross
gesture.note: The raised hand is the gesture of benediction; the triple cross is the mark of authority over the three worlds of body, mind, and spirit.

gaze.value: Facing forward, toward the viewer or the monks
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of the teacher, directed at the one who receives the teaching.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Hierophant's power is in transmission, not in motion.

centralObject.value: The triple cross and the crossed keys
centralObject.note: The cross is the symbol of the three worlds; the keys are the keys to sacred knowledge. Both are the instruments of the institution.

heldObject.value: The triple cross (left hand); the right hand is raised
heldObject.note: The cross is held as a symbol of authority; the raised hand is the gesture of blessing. The Hierophant holds the form and transmits the blessing.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Hierophant's world is the human, institutional world, not the animal world.

tool.value: The triple cross and the keys
tool.note: The tools are the instruments of the institution: the cross of authority and the keys of access.

writtenWord.value: Absent (the teaching is transmitted orally, through gesture and institution)
writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Hierophant's law is transmitted through the institution and the gesture, not through a book.

landscape.value: An institutional interior (temple or church)
landscape.note: The landscape is an interior, a sacred enclosure. The Hierophant is not in the open world; he is in the place where the teaching is kept.

architecture.note: The pillars are the architecture of the institution; the throne is the seat of authority. The Hierophant is established within a structure.

threshold.value: The threshold is the boundary of the institution
threshold.note: The threshold is the line between the inside and the outside, the faithful and the uninitiated. The Hierophant guards it.

celestialBody.note: There is no celestial body. The Hierophant's authority is institutional, not cosmic.

weather.note: There is no weather. The Hierophant is in an interior space, protected from the elements.

symmetry.value: Balanced and symmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the seated figure, the two pillars, the two monks. The symmetry is the point — the institution is a structure of balance.

repetitionCount.value: Two pillars, two monks, three tiers of the cross
repetitionCount.note: The repetitions are the repetitions of the institution: the two pillars, the two monks, the three worlds of the cross.

verticalAxis.value: The triple cross above, the keys below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the cross) to the earthly (the keys). The Hierophant is the point at which the teaching is transmitted from above to below.

horizontalAxis.value: The two monks kneel to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the plane of the community: the teacher in the centre, the receivers on either side.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Hierophant is upright and established.

clothing.value: Red and grey robes, a triple crown
clothing.note: Red is the colour of authority; grey is the colour of institution. The robes mark him as a figure of established tradition.

nudity.note: The Hierophant is fully clothed. His authority is mediated by form and institution.

crown.note: The triple crown is the mark of authority over the three worlds of body, mind, and spirit. It is a crown of institution, not of nature.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Hierophant is not suffering; he is transmitting.

binding.value: Absent (though the monks kneel, they are not bound)
binding.note: There are no chains. The Hierophant's authority is accepted, not imposed by force.

water.note: There is no water. The Hierophant's element is earth and spirit, not water.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Hierophant's heat is the heat of tradition, not of passion.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Hierophant's world is the built world, not the natural world.

stone.note: Stone is the material of the institution. The Hierophant's authority is built on stone, not on sand.

polarity.note: The Hierophant's remedy-pair is the Devil: he is tradition and institution, the Devil is instinct and the breaking of form. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Hierophant's institutional rigidity is the Devil's instinct: sometimes the inherited form needs to be broken by the raw energy of desire.

prescribedAct.value: Ask what you have inherited that still serves you, and what you are carrying only because it was handed to you.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of discernment. The Hierophant's lesson is that tradition is a gift, but not every gift must be kept.

detailedReading: The Hierophant is the card of the institution and the inherited form, and its detailed features show how that form is transmitted. Its elemental register is earth and spirit: the seated posture, the institutional setting, and the red and grey robes mark him as the card of established tradition. The numerical degree is five — the number of the human figure, the point at which the cosmic order becomes a social order — and the posture is seated on a throne, upright, between two pillars. The gesture is one of blessing and authority: the right hand raised, the left hand holding the triple cross. The central objects are the cross and the crossed keys: the symbol of the three worlds and the keys to sacred knowledge. The landscape is an institutional interior, a temple or church, and the architecture is the pillars and the throne. There is no creature, no written word, no celestial body, no wound, and no binding: the Hierophant's world is the human, institutional world, not the animal world; his law is transmitted through gesture, not through a book; his authority is institutional, not cosmic; he is not suffering; and his authority is accepted, not imposed by force. The symmetry of the composition confirms that the institution is a structure of balance. The prescribed act follows from this: ask what you have inherited that still serves you, and what you are carrying only because it was handed to you. The remedy is instinct — the Devil's raw energy — because the inherited form needs to be corrected by the capacity to break it.

name: The Lovers
symbols: A man and a woman stand beneath a winged angel — the human pair under the blessing of a larger unity.
Behind the woman, a tree with fruit — appetite, temptation, the knowledge of good and evil.
Behind the man, a tree with flames — passion, desire, the fire of the will.
A mountain rises between them — the obstacle or choice that the union must pass through.

reading.upright: The Lovers is union — of two people, of two parts of the self, or of one's actions with one's values. It is also the choice that such union requires.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Lovers point to misalignment: a relationship or a decision that does not match the deeper self, or avoidance of the choice.

elementalRegister.value: Air / Spirit (Major Arcana; the angel, the garden, the mountain)
elementalRegister.note: The Lovers is a Major Arcana card, and its element is spirit. The angel overhead and the garden setting mark it as the card of the union that is blessed from above and enacted on earth.

numericalDegree.note: Six is the number of harmony and balance. The Lovers is the sixth point, the moment at which two become a unity.

courtFunction.note: The Lovers is not a court card; it is the archetype of union and choice.

figureType.value: A man, a woman, and a winged angel
figureType.note: The human pair is the subject, but the angel marks the union as more than human: it is a union under a larger order.

posture.value: The man and woman stand facing forward or toward each other; the angel stands above with arms outstretched
posture.note: The posture of the humans is open and exposed; the angel's posture is one of blessing and inclusion.

gesture.value: The woman looks up at the angel; the man looks at the woman; the angel's arms are open
gesture.note: The gestures form a chain of attention: the woman attends to the divine, the man to the woman, the angel to both.

gaze.value: The woman gazes upward; the man gazes at the woman; the angel gazes downward
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of attraction and alignment. Each figure is looking at what is above or beside it.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Lovers is a card of presence and choice, not of action.

centralObject.value: The two trees (fruit and flame) and the mountain
centralObject.note: The trees are the two forms of desire: the fruit of appetite and the flame of passion. The mountain is the obstacle that the union must pass through.

heldObject.note: There is nothing held. The Lovers are not defined by what they carry but by what they are choosing.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Lovers is a card of human and divine relationship, not of instinct.

tool.note: There is no tool. The Lovers is a card of relationship, not of work.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Lovers' law is written in the heart, not in a book.

landscape.value: A garden with two trees and a mountain in the distance
landscape.note: The landscape is the garden of Eden, the place of innocence and choice. The mountain is the obstacle that the union must pass through.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Lovers are in the open garden, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: The mountain is the obstacle that the union must cross. It is the threshold between the garden and the world.

celestialBody.note: The angel is the celestial presence that blesses the union. It is the mark of the divine sanction of human love.

weather.note: The weather is fair. The Lovers are in a garden, not in a storm.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the man and woman on either side, the angel above)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the two humans on either side, the angel above them. The symmetry is the symmetry of union.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of polarity and union. The two trees and the two humans are the structural expression of the card's theme.

verticalAxis.value: The angel above, the humans below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the divine to the human. The Lovers are the point at which the two meet.

horizontalAxis.value: The man and woman to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of relationship: the two humans facing each other or facing forward together.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Lovers are upright and open.

clothing.value: The humans are nude or lightly clothed; the angel is robed
clothing.note: The nudity of the humans is the mark of innocence and exposure; the angel's robes are the mark of the divine.

nudity.value: Present (the human figures are nude or lightly clothed)
nudity.note: The nudity is the nudity of Eden: innocence, exposure, and the absence of shame.

crown.note: There is no crown. The Lovers are not figures of authority; they are figures of relationship.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Lovers are not suffering; they are choosing.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Lovers are free to choose.

water.note: There is no water. The Lovers' element is air and spirit, not water.

fire.value: The tree of flames behind the man
fire.note: The fire is the flame of passion and desire. It is one of the two forms of appetite that the Lovers must integrate.

vegetation.value: The tree of fruit and the tree of flames
vegetation.note: The vegetation is the two trees: the fruit of appetite and the flame of passion. Both are alive, both are part of the choice.

stone.note: Stone is present as the mountain, the obstacle that the union must pass through.

polarity.note: The Lovers' remedy-pair is the Devil: the Lovers are union under blessing, the Devil is bondage under shadow. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Lovers' idealism is the Devil's shadow: sometimes the union must confront what it has refused to see.

prescribedAct.value: Name the choice you are actually making, not the one you wish you were making.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of honesty. The Lovers' lesson is that union is not a feeling; it is a choice that must be made.

detailedReading: The Lovers is the card of union and choice, and its detailed features show how that union is structured. Its elemental register is air and spirit: the angel overhead, the garden setting, and the naked human figures mark it as the card of the union that is blessed from above and enacted on earth. The numerical degree is six — the number of harmony and balance — and the posture is standing and open. The gestures form a chain of attention: the woman looks up at the angel, the man looks at the woman, the angel's arms are open. The central objects are the two trees — the fruit of appetite and the flame of passion — and the mountain in the distance. The landscape is the garden of Eden, and the angel is the celestial presence that blesses the union. There is no architecture, no creature, no tool, no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Lovers are in the open garden, not in a city, not driven by instinct, not defined by work, not following a text, not suffering, and not bound. The symmetry of the composition confirms that the card is about the balance of two. The prescribed act follows from this: name the choice you are actually making, not the one you wish you were making. The remedy is shadow — the Devil's confrontation — because the union needs to be corrected by the capacity to see what it has refused.

name: The Chariot
symbols: An armored figure drives a chariot — force directed by a will that stays at the reins.
Two sphinxes, one black and one white, pull the chariot — opposing forces, reconciled by the driver's hand.
A starry canopy hangs above — the cosmic support of a well-aimed action.
A walled city recedes behind him — the safety he has left in order to move.

reading.upright: The Chariot is directed will — the capacity to hold opposing forces together long enough to move. Victory through discipline, momentum, and clear aim.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Chariot's force scatters: no clear destination, the reins dropped, or aggression mistaken for direction.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the chariot, the sphinxes, the starry canopy)
elementalRegister.note: The Chariot is a Major Arcana card, and its element is spirit, but the imagery of the chariot and the sphinxes marks it as the card of directed motion, the will that holds opposing forces together.

numericalDegree.note: Seven is the number of victory and completion. The Chariot is the seventh point, the moment at which the will achieves its aim.

courtFunction.note: The Chariot is not a court card; it is the archetype of directed will and victory.

figureType.value: An armoured human figure driving a chariot
figureType.note: He is human and armoured, a driver rather than a passenger. His armour marks him as a figure of war and discipline.

posture.value: Standing upright in the chariot, holding the reins
posture.note: The upright posture is the posture of control. The Charioteer is not seated; he is standing, alert, and in command.

gesture.value: Holding the reins of the two sphinxes
gesture.note: The gesture is one of control: the reins are held, not dropped. The Charioteer is the point at which the opposing forces are held together.

gaze.value: Facing forward, toward the direction of travel
gaze.note: The gaze is fixed on the destination. The Charioteer is not looking back at the city he has left.

movementDirection.note: The movement is rightward, toward the future. The Chariot is the card of directed progress.

centralObject.value: The chariot and the two sphinxes
centralObject.note: The chariot is the vehicle of the will; the sphinxes are the opposing forces that must be reconciled for the vehicle to move.

heldObject.note: The reins are the instrument of control. The Charioteer holds them, not the sphinxes.

creature.value: Two sphinxes, one black and one white
creature.note: The sphinxes are the opposing forces: the black and the white, the conscious and the unconscious. They are not enemies; they are the paired energies that the will must hold together.

tool.note: The tools are the instruments of direction: the vehicle and the means of controlling it.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Charioteer's law is written in his aim, not in a book.

landscape.value: A walled city recedes behind him; the way ahead is open
landscape.note: The landscape is the city that has been left and the open road ahead. The Charioteer is moving away from safety and toward the unknown.

architecture.note: The city is the architecture of safety and community. The Charioteer has left it in order to move.

threshold.value: The city gate is the threshold
threshold.note: The gate is the threshold between the safety of the city and the danger of the road. The Charioteer has crossed it.

celestialBody.note: The stars are the cosmic support of a well-aimed action. They mark the Chariot as a card of destiny as well as will.

weather.note: The weather is fair. The Chariot is not moving through a storm; the difficulty is in the direction, not the conditions.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the two sphinxes on either side, the driver in the centre)
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the two sphinxes, the driver, the chariot. The symmetry is the point — the Chariot is the balance of opposing forces.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of polarity. The two sphinxes are the structural expression of the card's theme of held opposition.

verticalAxis.value: The starry canopy above, the chariot below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the cosmic (the stars) to the earthly (the chariot). The Charioteer is the point of connection.

horizontalAxis.value: The two sphinxes to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of motion: the two sphinxes pulling the chariot forward.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Charioteer is upright and in control.

clothing.value: Armour with a starry canopy
clothing.note: The armour is the mark of readiness; the starry canopy is the mark of cosmic support. The Charioteer is dressed for both war and destiny.

nudity.note: The Charioteer is fully clothed and armoured. His power is mediated by form and protection.

crown.value: A crown (implied by his status as a driver of sphinxes)
crown.note: The crown is the mark of authority. The Charioteer is a figure of command, not of service.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Charioteer is not suffering; he is commanding.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Charioteer is free to move.

water.value: Absent (the sphinxes are creatures of land and air, not water)
water.note: There is no water. The Chariot's element is spirit and air, not water.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Chariot's heat is the heat of will, not of passion.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Chariot is on the road, not in a garden.

stone.value: The walls of the city behind him
stone.note: Stone is present as the city walls, the architecture of safety that has been left behind.

polarity.note: The Chariot's remedy-pair is Strength: he is directed will, she is gentle mastery. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Chariot's force is Strength's gentleness: sometimes the opposing forces are held together not by the reins but by patience.

prescribedAct.value: Choose one direction and hold to it today, even when the forces pull against each other.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of direction. The Chariot's lesson is that victory is not the absence of opposition but the holding of it.

detailedReading: The Chariot is the card of directed will and victory, and its detailed features show how that will is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the chariot, the sphinxes, and the starry canopy mark it as the card of directed motion, the will that holds opposing forces together. The numerical degree is seven — the number of victory and completion — and the posture is standing upright in the chariot, holding the reins. The gesture is one of control: the reins are held, not dropped. The central objects are the chariot and the two sphinxes, one black and one white. The sphinxes are the opposing forces, the conscious and the unconscious, the black and the white; they are not enemies but paired energies that the will must hold. The landscape is the walled city that recedes behind him and the open road ahead. The starry canopy is the cosmic support of a well-aimed action. There is no creature other than the sphinxes, no tool other than the chariot and reins, no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Charioteer is not driven by instinct, not defined by work, not following a text, not suffering, and not bound. The symmetry of the composition confirms that the card is about the balance of opposing forces. The prescribed act follows from this: choose one direction and hold to it today, even when the forces pull against each other. The remedy is gentleness — Strength's patience — because the directed will needs to be corrected by the capacity to hold without force.

name: Strength
symbols: A woman calmly opens (or closes) a lion's jaws — not force, but the gentle mastery of a wild thing.
The infinity symbol hovers above her head — limitless patience, an inner resource without end.
She is dressed in white — purity of intention, the calm that gentleness requires.
The lion itself is the passion she handles — not killed, but befriended.

reading.upright: Strength is inner power, not force: the courage to meet one's own wildness with patience, to master by gentleness. It favours softness over struggle.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the lion is running the show — self-doubt, raw impulse, or the fear that gentleness is weakness.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; the lion, the white robe, the infinity symbol)
elementalRegister.note: Strength is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by fire: the lion, the white robe, and the infinity symbol mark it as the card of inner courage and the gentle mastery of passion.

numericalDegree.note: Eight is the number of balance and regeneration. Strength is the eighth point, the moment at which the wild energy is brought into harmony.

courtFunction.note: Strength is not a court card; it is the archetype of inner courage and gentle mastery.

figureType.value: A human woman and a lion
figureType.note: The woman is human; the lion is the animal self. The card is the meeting of the two, not the conquest of one by the other.

posture.value: The woman stands or kneels calmly, her hands on the lion's jaws
posture.note: The posture is one of calm and control. She is not struggling; she is holding the lion's jaws with patience.

gesture.value: Hands opening or closing the lion's jaws
gesture.note: The gesture is one of gentle mastery: she is not forcing the jaws open or shut; she is holding them, and the lion is calmed.

gaze.value: The woman looks at the lion or at the jaws; the lion may look at her
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of recognition. She is not avoiding the lion's eyes; she is meeting them.

movementDirection.value: Static (the woman is calm, the lion is calmed)
movementDirection.note: There is no movement. Strength is the card of the still point at which the wild energy is held.

centralObject.value: The lion's jaws and the infinity symbol
centralObject.note: The jaws are the wild energy; the infinity symbol is the limitless patience that holds it.

heldObject.note: She holds the jaws, but she does not grip them. The holding is an act of patience, not of force.

creature.note: The lion is the animal self, the passion and the wildness. It is not an enemy; it is the energy that must be befriended.

tool.note: Her only tool is her hands. Strength is not a card of instruments; it is a card of direct, patient contact.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. Strength's law is written in the body and the gesture, not in a book.

landscape.value: A landscape with mountains in the background
landscape.note: The landscape is open and natural, with mountains in the distance. It is the world in which the wild energy is met.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. Strength is in the open world, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: There is no threshold. Strength is not crossing from one state to another; she is at the centre of the meeting.

celestialBody.value: The infinity symbol above her head
celestialBody.note: The infinity symbol is the celestial mark of limitless patience. It is not a sun or a moon; it is the sign of the endless resource of gentleness.

weather.note: The weather is fair. Strength is not in a storm; the difficulty is in the meeting, not the conditions.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the woman and the lion are the two poles)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced between the woman and the lion. The symmetry is the symmetry of the meeting of two energies.

repetitionCount.note: The number one is the number of the single meeting. Strength is not about many forces; it is about the one wild energy and the one patient hand.

verticalAxis.value: The infinity symbol above, the lion below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the infinite patience above to the wild energy below. The woman is the point of connection.

horizontalAxis.value: The woman and the lion face each other
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of meeting: the woman on one side, the lion on the other.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The woman is upright, the lion is calm.

clothing.value: A white robe
clothing.note: White is the colour of purity and calm. The robe marks her as a figure of gentleness, not of force.

nudity.note: She is clothed. Her power is mediated by calm, not by exposure.

crown.note: She wears no crown, but the infinity symbol is the mark of limitless patience. Her authority is not social but inner.

wound.note: There is no wound. Strength is not suffering; she is mastering.

binding.note: There are no chains. The lion is not bound; it is calmed.

water.note: There is no water. Strength's element is fire and spirit, not water.

fire.note: The lion is the fire of passion. It is not extinguished; it is befriended.

vegetation.note: The vegetation is present but not dominant. The card is about the meeting of human and animal, not about the garden.

stone.note: Stone is present as the mountains, the distant obstacles that the mastered energy can now face.

polarity.note: Strength's remedy-pair is the Chariot: she is gentle mastery, he is directed will. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for Strength's gentleness is the Chariot's direction: sometimes the calmed energy needs to be aimed at a goal.

prescribedAct.value: Meet one wild impulse today with patience rather than force, and see what happens.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of gentleness. Strength's lesson is that the wild energy is not to be killed but to be befriended.

detailedReading: Strength is the card of inner courage and gentle mastery, and its detailed features show how that mastery is achieved. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the lion, the white robe, and the infinity symbol mark it as the card of inner courage and the gentle mastery of passion. The numerical degree is eight — the number of balance and regeneration — and the posture is calm, the woman standing or kneeling with her hands on the lion's jaws. The gesture is one of gentle mastery: she is not forcing the jaws; she is holding them, and the lion is calmed. The central objects are the lion's jaws and the infinity symbol: the wild energy and the limitless patience that holds it. The creature is the lion, the animal self, the passion that must be befriended. The landscape is open, with mountains in the distance. There is no architecture, no threshold, no written word, no wound, and no binding: Strength is in the open world, not crossing a boundary, not following a text, not suffering, and not bound. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the meeting of two energies. The prescribed act follows from this: meet one wild impulse today with patience rather than force, and see what happens. The remedy is direction — the Chariot's aim — because the calmed energy needs to be corrected by the capacity to direct it.

name: The Hermit
symbols: An old man stands alone on a snowy peak — elevation, the long climb toward understanding.
He holds a lantern in which a single star burns — his own inner light, carried into the dark.
A staff supports him — the simple, unglamorous support that makes the journey possible.
His back is turned to us — the inward direction of his attention.

reading.upright: The Hermit is deliberate solitude — the withdrawal that lets one hear oneself. Wisdom earned by looking inward, and the willingness to walk alone for a time.
reading.reversed: Reversed, solitude has become isolation: the withdrawal that no longer returns, or a loneliness that hides rather than seeks.

elementalRegister.value: Earth / Spirit (Major Arcana; the snowy peak, the staff, the lantern)
elementalRegister.note: The Hermit is a Major Arcana card, but his imagery is dominated by earth: the snowy peak, the staff, and the lantern mark him as the card of deliberate solitude and the slow accumulation of wisdom.

numericalDegree.note: Nine is the number of completion and the threshold of a new cycle. The Hermit is the ninth point, the moment at which the inner work is brought to a kind of completion.

courtFunction.note: The Hermit is not a court card; he is the archetype of solitude and inner guidance.

figureType.value: An old human man, alone, on a snowy peak
figureType.note: He is human and aged, alone on a height. His age marks him as a figure of experience, not of youth.

posture.value: Standing upright, leaning on a staff, facing away or inward
posture.note: The posture is one of deliberate solitude: he is not moving toward the viewer; he is standing on his own ground.

gesture.value: One hand holds the lantern; the other holds the staff
gesture.note: The lantern is the inner light; the staff is the simple support. The gestures are those of a traveller who carries his own light and his own support.

gaze.value: Looking inward or downward, not at the viewer
gaze.note: The gaze is inward. The Hermit is looking at what is within, not at what is without.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Hermit's power is in stillness and introspection, not in travel.

centralObject.value: The lantern with a single star
centralObject.note: The lantern is the inner light, the wisdom that is carried into the dark. The star is the single point of certainty within it.

heldObject.note: The lantern is the light; the staff is the support. Both are held, both are necessary.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Hermit's solitude is complete; he is not accompanied by an animal self.

tool.note: The tools are the instruments of solitary travel: the light and the support.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Hermit's wisdom is not written in a book; it is carried in the lantern.

landscape.value: A snowy mountain peak
landscape.note: The landscape is the height, the place of elevation and solitude. The snow marks it as a place of cold and clarity.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Hermit is on the bare peak, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: The peak is the threshold between the world below and the sky above. The Hermit stands at the point of separation.

celestialBody.value: The star in the lantern (a celestial light brought down)
celestialBody.note: The star is the celestial body, but it is contained within the lantern. The Hermit carries the cosmos within him.

weather.note: The weather is cold and clear. The Hermit's clarity is the clarity of the cold, not the warmth of the hearth.

symmetry.value: Asymmetrical (the figure is alone, the composition is off-centre)
symmetry.note: The composition is asymmetrical. The Hermit is a solitary figure, not a balanced pair.

repetitionCount.value: One of each (one lantern, one star, one staff)
repetitionCount.note: The number one is the number of solitude. The Hermit is alone with his single light and his single support.

verticalAxis.value: The peak above, the world below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the axis of elevation: the Hermit is above the world, closer to the sky.

horizontalAxis.value: The figure is alone, facing inward
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of isolation: there is no one beside him.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Hermit is upright, though his gaze is inward.

clothing.value: Grey robes and a hood
clothing.note: Grey is the colour of the solitary and the humble. The hood marks him as a figure of withdrawal.

nudity.note: The Hermit is fully clothed. His solitude is mediated by the robes of the wanderer.

crown.note: There is no crown. The Hermit has no social authority; his authority is inner.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Hermit is not suffering; he is contemplating.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Hermit is free, and his freedom is the freedom of solitude.

water.note: There is no water. The Hermit's element is earth and spirit, not water.

fire.value: The lantern's light (a small, contained fire)
fire.note: The fire is contained within the lantern. It is the small, steady light of inner wisdom, not the blaze of passion.

vegetation.value: Absent (the peak is bare and snowy)
vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Hermit's world is bare and cold, stripped of the distractions of growth.

stone.note: Stone is the material of the peak. The Hermit's wisdom is built on the hard ground of solitude.

polarity.note: The Hermit's remedy-pair is the Lovers: he is solitude, they are union. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Hermit's isolation is the Lovers' union: sometimes the withdrawal needs to be corrected by the return to relationship.

prescribedAct.value: Spend one hour alone today without distraction, and listen for the small light you are carrying.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of solitude. The Hermit's lesson is that wisdom is not found in the crowd; it is found in the quiet.

detailedReading: The Hermit is the card of deliberate solitude and inner guidance, and its detailed features show how that solitude is structured. Its elemental register is earth and spirit: the snowy peak, the staff, and the lantern mark him as the card of deliberate solitude and the slow accumulation of wisdom. The numerical degree is nine — the number of completion and the threshold of a new cycle — and the posture is standing upright, leaning on a staff, facing inward. The gesture is one of holding both the light and the support: the lantern in one hand, the staff in the other. The gaze is inward, not at the viewer. The central object is the lantern with a single star, the inner light carried into the dark. The landscape is a snowy mountain peak, the place of elevation and solitude. There is no architecture, no creature, no written word, no crown, no wound, and no binding: the Hermit is on the bare peak, not in a city, not accompanied by an animal, not following a text, not a figure of social authority, not suffering, and not bound. The asymmetry of the composition confirms that he is a solitary figure. The prescribed act follows from this: spend one hour alone today without distraction, and listen for the small light you are carrying. The remedy is connection — the Lovers' union — because the solitude needs to be corrected by the capacity to return.

name: Wheel of Fortune
symbols: A great wheel turns in the sky — the law of return, the cycle no one escapes.
A sphinx sits atop the wheel with a sword — the riddle, and the balance the wheel demands.
A serpent descends on one side while Anubis rises on the other — descent and ascent, the twin motions of fortune.
Four winged creatures hold the corners — the four elements, the fixed points that the turning wheel requires.

reading.upright: The Wheel of Fortune is the turning of cycles — the recognition that fate, luck and time move in patterns larger than the will. A turning point.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the wheel is resisted or repeating: bad luck, or the same pattern returning because it has not been understood.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; the wheel, the sphinx, the four creatures)
elementalRegister.note: The Wheel of Fortune is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by fire: the wheel, the sphinx, and the four creatures mark it as the card of the turning cycle, the law of return.

numericalDegree.note: Ten is the number of completion and the return to the beginning. The Wheel is the tenth point, the moment at which the cycle completes itself.

courtFunction.note: The Wheel of Fortune is not a court card; it is the archetype of the turning cycle.

figureType.value: A sphinx, a serpent, Anubis, and four winged creatures
