figureType.note: The figures are not human. They are the cosmic and animal forces that turn the wheel: the sphinx, the serpent, the jackal-headed Anubis, and the four creatures of the elements.

posture.value: The sphinx sits atop the wheel; the serpent descends; Anubis rises; the four creatures hold the corners
posture.note: The postures are the postures of the cycle: the sphinx at the still point, the serpent descending, Anubis ascending, the four creatures fixed at the corners.

gesture.value: The sphinx holds a sword; the serpent and Anubis are in motion; the four creatures hold the corners
gesture.note: The gestures are the gestures of the turning: the sword is the point of balance, the serpent and Anubis are the twin motions of descent and ascent.

gaze.value: The sphinx looks outward; the creatures look toward the wheel
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of witness. The figures are watching the wheel turn, not controlling it.

movementDirection.note: The movement is circular, the movement of the cycle. The Wheel is the card of return, not of linear progress.

centralObject.value: The wheel
centralObject.note: The wheel is the central object, the law of return. It is the structure of fortune itself.

heldObject.note: The sword is the point of balance, the clarity that the turning wheel requires.

creature.value: Sphinx, serpent, Anubis, and four winged creatures (lion, bull, eagle, man)
creature.note: The creatures are the cosmic and elemental forces: the sphinx is the riddle, the serpent is descent, Anubis is ascent, the four creatures are the fixed elements.

tool.note: The sword is the tool of clarity. It is the point at which the turning wheel is understood.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Wheel's law is written in the turning itself, not in a book.

landscape.value: A sky with clouds and a wheel
landscape.note: The landscape is the sky, the realm of the cosmic. The Wheel is not on the earth; it is in the heavens.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Wheel is in the open sky, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: The wheel is the threshold between one cycle and the next. It is the point of turning.

celestialBody.value: Clouds and the sky (the wheel itself is the celestial body)
celestialBody.note: The wheel is the celestial body. It is the structure of the heavens, the law of return.

weather.note: The weather is cloudy and turbulent. The Wheel is not a card of calm; it is a card of change.

symmetry.value: Circular (the wheel is symmetrical)
symmetry.note: The composition is circular and symmetrical. The symmetry is the symmetry of the cycle.

repetitionCount.note: The number four is the number of the fixed points. The four creatures are the corners of the turning world.

verticalAxis.value: The sphinx above, the wheel below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the sphinx (the riddle) to the wheel (the cycle). The sphinx is the still point above the turning.

horizontalAxis.value: The serpent on one side, Anubis on the other
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of descent and ascent: the serpent descending, Anubis rising.

inversion.value: Present (the serpent descends, Anubis rises — the wheel turns both ways)
inversion.note: The inversion is the inversion of the cycle: what goes up comes down, what goes down comes up.

clothing.value: Absent (the creatures are not clothed)
clothing.note: The creatures are not clothed. The Wheel is a card of cosmic forces, not of human society.

nudity.value: Present (the creatures are nude or unclothed)
nudity.note: The nudity is the nudity of the cosmic: the forces are exposed, not mediated by culture.

crown.note: There is no crown. The Wheel is not a card of social authority.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Wheel is not a card of suffering; it is a card of change.

binding.note: There are no chains. The wheel turns freely.

water.note: There is no water. The Wheel's element is fire and spirit, not water.

fire.value: The wheel itself (the fire of change)
fire.note: The fire is the fire of change, the heat of the turning cycle.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Wheel is in the sky, not in a garden.

stone.note: There is no stone. The Wheel is not built; it turns.

polarity.note: The Wheel of Fortune's remedy-pair is Justice: the Wheel is the turning of fortune, Justice is the principle of consequence. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Wheel's randomness is Justice's consequence: sometimes the turning must be understood as the working out of what has been done.

prescribedAct.value: Name the cycle you are in, and ask what it is asking you to learn before it turns again.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of recognition. The Wheel's lesson is that the cycle is not random; it is a pattern that can be understood.

detailedReading: The Wheel of Fortune is the card of the turning cycle, and its detailed features show how that cycle is structured. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the wheel, the sphinx, and the four creatures mark it as the card of the turning cycle, the law of return. The numerical degree is ten — the number of completion and the return to the beginning — and the posture is the posture of the cycle: the sphinx at the still point, the serpent descending, Anubis ascending, the four creatures fixed at the corners. The central object is the wheel itself, the structure of fortune. The creatures are the cosmic and elemental forces: the sphinx is the riddle, the serpent is descent, Anubis is ascent, the four creatures are the fixed elements. The landscape is the sky, the realm of the cosmic, and the weather is cloudy and turbulent. There is no architecture, no threshold, no written word, no crown, no wound, and no binding: the Wheel is in the open sky, not in a city, not crossing a boundary, not following a text, not a figure of social authority, not suffering, and not bound. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the cycle. The prescribed act follows from this: name the cycle you are in, and ask what it is asking you to learn before it turns again. The remedy is consequence — Justice's principle — because the turning must be corrected by the understanding of what it is working out.

name: Justice
symbols: She holds a sword perfectly upright — reason, cutting cleanly through what is unclear.
In her other hand, scales — the careful weighing of what cannot be decided by force.
She wears a crown — truth has authority here.
A red robe falls from her shoulders — the active, living quality of real judgment.

reading.upright: Justice is the principle of consequence: what is true, what is fair, and what follows from what. It asks for honest accounting and clear sight.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Justice is miscarried: dishonesty, imbalance, or the refusal to face a consequence. It asks where the scale is being hidden.

elementalRegister.value: Air / Spirit (Major Arcana; the sword, the scales, the crown)
elementalRegister.note: Justice is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by air: the sword, the scales, and the crown mark it as the card of clear judgment and honest accounting.

numericalDegree.note: Eleven is the number of the new cycle, the point at which the old is weighed and the new is decided. Justice is the eleventh point, the moment of judgment.

courtFunction.note: Justice is not a court card; she is the archetype of fair judgment.

figureType.value: A seated human woman holding a sword and scales
figureType.note: She is human and seated, a figure of authority. Her posture marks her as a judge, not a warrior.

posture.value: Seated upright, holding the sword and scales
posture.note: The seated posture is the posture of deliberation. Justice is not rushing; she is weighing.

gesture.value: Right hand holds the sword upright; left hand holds the scales
gesture.note: The sword is the instrument of clarity; the scales are the instrument of balance. The gestures are those of a judge who cuts and weighs.

gaze.value: Facing forward, direct and impartial
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of impartial judgment. Justice is not looking at one side or the other; she is looking at what is true.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. Justice's power is in deliberation, not in motion.

centralObject.value: The sword and the scales
centralObject.note: The sword is the instrument of clarity; the scales are the instrument of balance. Together they are the tools of judgment.

heldObject.note: The sword is held upright, the scales are held level. The held objects are the instruments of fair decision.

creature.note: There is no creature. Justice is a card of human and cosmic law, not of instinct.

tool.note: The tools are the instruments of judgment: the sword that cuts through falsehood, the scales that weigh what is true.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. Justice's law is not written in a book; it is enacted in the gesture of weighing.

landscape.value: A veil or curtain behind her
landscape.note: The landscape is an interior, a place of judgment. The veil marks it as a space set apart.

architecture.value: A throne or seat of judgment
architecture.note: The architecture is the seat of judgment. Justice is established in a place of authority.

threshold.note: There is no threshold. Justice is at the centre of her deliberation, not crossing into another state.

celestialBody.note: There is no celestial body. Justice's authority is not derived from the heavens; it is established in the act of judgment.

weather.note: There is no weather. Justice is in an interior space, protected from the elements, where the only climate is the climate of the mind.

symmetry.value: Balanced and symmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the sword and the scales, the seated figure. The symmetry is the point — Justice is the balance of the two.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of balance. The two tools are the structural expression of the card's theme.

verticalAxis.value: The sword upright, the scales level
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the axis of the sword; the horizontal axis is the axis of the scales. Justice holds both.

horizontalAxis.value: The scales held level
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of balance: the scales are held level, not tipped.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. Justice is upright and balanced.

clothing.value: Red robes and a crown
clothing.note: Red is the colour of active judgment; the crown is the mark of authority. Justice is dressed as a judge.

nudity.note: Justice is fully clothed. Her authority is mediated by form and institution.

crown.note: The crown is the mark of authority. Justice's truth has authority.

wound.note: There is no wound. Justice is not suffering; she is judging.

binding.note: There are no chains. Justice is free to judge.

water.note: There is no water. Justice's element is air and spirit, not water.

fire.value: Absent (the red robes are the colour of fire, but there is no flame)
fire.note: Fire is present as colour, not as flame. Justice's heat is the heat of judgment, not of passion.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. Justice's world is the world of law, not of nature.

stone.value: The throne or seat of judgment
stone.note: Stone is the material of the seat of judgment. Justice's authority is built on stone, not on sand.

polarity.note: Justice's remedy-pair is the Wheel of Fortune: she is consequence, the Wheel is the turning of fortune. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for Justice's rigidity is the Wheel's acceptance of chance: sometimes not everything is a consequence; some things simply turn.

prescribedAct.value: Weigh one decision today with the scales, not the sword: ask what is fair, not what is fast.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of deliberation. Justice's lesson is that judgment is not punishment; it is the act of seeing clearly.

detailedReading: Justice is the card of fair judgment and honest accounting, and its detailed features show how that judgment is structured. Its elemental register is air and spirit: the sword, the scales, and the crown mark it as the card of clear judgment. The numerical degree is eleven — the number of the new cycle, the point at which the old is weighed and the new is decided — and the posture is seated upright, holding the sword and the scales. The gesture is one of cutting and weighing: the sword held upright, the scales held level. The central objects are the sword and the scales: the instruments of clarity and balance. The landscape is an interior, a place of judgment. There is no creature, no written word, no threshold, no celestial body, no wound, and no binding: Justice is a card of human and cosmic law, not of instinct; her law is enacted, not written; she is at the centre of her deliberation; her authority is established in the act of judgment; she is not suffering; and she is free to judge. The symmetry of the composition confirms that she is the balance of the two tools. The prescribed act follows from this: weigh one decision today with the scales, not the sword: ask what is fair, not what is fast. The remedy is the acceptance of chance — the Wheel's turning — because the judgment needs to be corrected by the recognition that not everything is a consequence.

name: The Hanged Man
symbols: A figure hangs upside down from a living tree — a reversal that is chosen, not suffered.
A halo glows around his head — illumination arriving through the inversion.
His legs form a triangle — stability within the suspension.
His face is calm — the absence of struggle that makes the reversal possible.

reading.upright: The Hanged Man is willing suspension: stopping, hanging between, and letting a new perspective arrive. Sacrifice that is chosen rather than imposed.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Hanged Man has become a stalling: an avoidance disguised as patience, or a sacrifice that has curdled into martyrdom.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the living tree, the halo, the suspended figure)
elementalRegister.note: The Hanged Man is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by water: the living tree, the halo, and the suspended figure mark it as the card of willing suspension and the new perspective that arrives through inversion.

numericalDegree.note: Twelve is the number of completion and the return to the beginning. The Hanged Man is the twelfth point, the moment at which the cycle is suspended and the new perspective is possible.

courtFunction.note: The Hanged Man is not a court card; he is the archetype of willing suspension.

figureType.value: A human man, suspended upside down from a living tree
figureType.note: He is human and inverted, suspended from a tree. His inversion is the central fact of the card.

posture.value: Suspended upside down, one leg crossed over the other, arms behind his back
posture.note: The posture is one of willing suspension. He is not struggling; he is hanging, and the hanging is chosen.

gesture.value: Arms behind his back, one leg crossed over the other
gesture.note: The gesture is one of non-resistance. His hands are not free, but he is not fighting the bonds.

gaze.value: Facing forward or slightly upward, calm
gaze.note: The gaze is calm and inward. He is not looking at the world in the ordinary way; he is seeing from a new angle.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Hanged Man is the card of the pause, the suspension between one state and another.

centralObject.value: The living tree and the suspended figure
centralObject.note: The tree is the living world; the figure is the one who has chosen to hang from it. The tree is not dead; it is alive, and the suspension is a living act.

heldObject.value: Absent (the arms are behind the back)
heldObject.note: There is nothing held. The Hanged Man has let go of the tools and the possessions of the ordinary world.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Hanged Man's suspension is a human act, not an instinctual one.

tool.value: Absent (the tree is not a tool)
tool.note: There is no tool. The Hanged Man has set aside the instruments of action.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Hanged Man's knowledge is not written; it is arrived at through suspension.

landscape.value: A living tree, a bare background
landscape.note: The landscape is the tree and the space around it. The background is bare, marking the suspension as a stripping away of distractions.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Hanged Man is suspended in the open, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.note: The suspension is the threshold between the ordinary perspective and the new one. The Hanged Man is between states.

celestialBody.note: The halo is the celestial mark of illumination. It is not a sun or a moon; it is the light that arrives through the inversion.

weather.note: The weather is clear. The Hanged Man is not in a storm; the difficulty is in the suspension, not the conditions.

symmetry.value: Asymmetrical (the figure is inverted, the composition is off-centre)
symmetry.note: The composition is asymmetrical. The Hanged Man is an inverted figure, not a balanced one.

repetitionCount.note: The number one is the number of the single act. The Hanged Man is alone with his suspension.

verticalAxis.value: The figure hangs below the tree
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is inverted: the figure hangs below the branch, and his head is closer to the ground than his feet.

horizontalAxis.value: The tree extends to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the tree, the living world from which he hangs.

inversion.note: The inversion is the central feature of the card. The Hanged Man is seeing the world from a new angle, and the inversion is the means by which the new perspective is achieved.

clothing.value: A simple tunic, blue and red
clothing.note: The clothing is simple, marking him as a figure who has stripped away the ordinary markers of status. The blue and red are the colours of water and fire, the elements of the inner life.

nudity.note: The Hanged Man is not nude, but he is lightly clothed. His vulnerability is not exposure but suspension.

crown.note: He wears no crown, but the halo is the mark of illumination. His authority is not social but spiritual.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Hanged Man is not suffering; he is suspended.

binding.value: Present (the rope or binding that suspends him)
binding.note: The binding is the rope that holds him to the tree. It is not a chain of oppression; it is the means of the suspension.

water.note: There is no water. The Hanged Man's element is water and spirit, but the water is not shown; it is the water of the inner life.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Hanged Man's heat is the heat of the inner illumination, not of passion.

vegetation.note: The tree is the living world. It is not dead; it is the support from which the Hanged Man hangs.

stone.note: There is no stone. The Hanged Man is not on the ground; he is suspended above it.

polarity.note: The Hanged Man's remedy-pair is the Magician: he is suspension, the Magician is action. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Hanged Man's suspension is the Magician's act: sometimes the pause must be broken by a deliberate gesture.

prescribedAct.value: Suspend one judgment today and look at the situation from the opposite angle.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of inversion. The Hanged Man's lesson is that the new perspective is not arrived at by effort; it is arrived at by letting go.

detailedReading: The Hanged Man is the card of willing suspension and new perspective, and its detailed features show how that suspension is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the living tree, the halo, and the suspended figure mark it as the card of willing suspension and the new perspective that arrives through inversion. The numerical degree is twelve — the number of completion and the return to the beginning — and the posture is suspended upside down, one leg crossed over the other, arms behind the back. The gesture is one of non-resistance: the hands are not free, but he is not fighting the bonds. The gaze is calm and inward. The central object is the living tree, the support from which he hangs. The landscape is the tree and the bare background. There is no creature, no tool, no written word, no crown, no wound, and the binding is the rope of suspension, not a chain of oppression. The inversion is the central feature of the card: the Hanged Man is seeing the world from a new angle. The prescribed act follows from this: suspend one judgment today and look at the situation from the opposite angle. The remedy is action — the Magician's gesture — because the suspension needs to be corrected by the capacity to act.

name: Death
symbols: A skeleton rides a white horse — the inescapable change, coming regardless of rank or preparation.
He carries a black banner with a white rose — the end, marked by purity rather than horror.
A king lies fallen beneath the horse — no position survives the change.
Between two towers the sun rises — a new dawn that can only appear once the old has passed.

reading.upright: Death is transformation, not literal death: the ending that makes the next form possible. Release, change, and the clearing away of what has finished.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Death is resisted: change refused, a stage clung to after it has ended, and the resulting stagnation.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the skeleton, the white horse, the rising sun)
elementalRegister.note: Death is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by water: the skeleton, the white horse, and the rising sun mark it as the card of transformation and the ending that makes the next form possible.

numericalDegree.note: Thirteen is the number of transformation and the end of a cycle. Death is the thirteenth point, the moment at which the old form is dissolved.

courtFunction.note: Death is not a court card; it is the archetype of transformation.

figureType.value: A skeleton on a white horse, with a king fallen beneath
figureType.note: The skeleton is the figure of death, the horseman of the apocalypse. The fallen king is the human figure who cannot escape the change.

posture.value: The skeleton rides upright on the horse; the king lies fallen
posture.note: The posture of the skeleton is one of inevitability; the posture of the king is one of defeat. The two postures are the two sides of the card.

gesture.value: The skeleton carries a black banner with a white rose
gesture.note: The banner is the gesture of the end. The white rose on the black banner is the mark of purity within the ending.

gaze.value: The skeleton faces forward; the king looks up or away
gaze.note: The gaze of the skeleton is the gaze of inevitability; the gaze of the king is the gaze of the one who cannot escape.

movementDirection.note: The movement is forward, the movement of the inescapable change. Death does not stop; it advances.

centralObject.value: The black banner with the white rose
centralObject.note: The banner is the central object. The black is the colour of the end; the white rose is the colour of purity. The ending is not horror; it is a clearing.

heldObject.note: The banner is held aloft. It is the standard of the change that cannot be resisted.

creature.note: The horse is the creature of the apocalypse. It is white, the colour of purity, and it carries the skeleton forward.

tool.note: The tool is the banner, not a sword. Death does not kill with a weapon; it announces the end.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. Death's law is not written; it is enacted.

landscape.value: A landscape with two towers and a rising sun
landscape.note: The landscape is the world that is being left and the world that is being born. The two towers are the old structures; the rising sun is the new dawn.

architecture.note: The towers are the architecture of the old world. They are the structures that the change is passing between.

threshold.value: The passage between the two towers is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the passage between the old and the new. Death is the crossing.

celestialBody.note: The sun is the celestial body of the new dawn. It rises between the two towers, marking the beginning that follows the end.

weather.value: Clear and bright (the sun is rising)
weather.note: The weather is clear. The sun is rising; the ending is also a beginning.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the skeleton in the centre, the towers on either side)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the skeleton in the centre, the towers on either side, the sun between them. The symmetry is the symmetry of the passage.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of the passage. The two towers mark the threshold between the old and the new.

verticalAxis.value: The skeleton above, the fallen king below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the axis of the fall: the skeleton rides above, the king lies below.

horizontalAxis.value: The two towers on either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the passage: the two towers mark the way through.

inversion.value: Present (the king is fallen, the order is inverted)
inversion.note: The inversion is the inversion of the social order: the king, who was above, is now below.

clothing.value: The skeleton is unclothed; the king is in robes
clothing.note: The skeleton is unclothed, marking the stripping away of all rank. The king's robes are the robes of the old order, which cannot survive the change.

nudity.note: The skeleton is nude. Death strips away all clothing, all rank, all pretense.

crown.value: The king's crown is fallen or removed
crown.note: The crown is the mark of social authority, and it is fallen. Death is the card that shows the limits of all social power.

wound.value: Absent (the skeleton is not wounded; it is the wound)
wound.note: There is no wound, but the skeleton is the mark of the end. The wound is the change itself.

binding.note: There are no chains. Death is not bound; it is the unbinding.

water.note: There is no water. Death's element is water and spirit, but the water is not shown; it is the water of the transformation.

fire.note: There is no fire. Death's heat is the heat of the change, not of passion.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. Death is the card of the bare ground that precedes the new growth.

stone.note: Stone is present as the two towers, the architecture of the old world.

polarity.note: Death's remedy-pair is the Star: he is the end, she is the healing. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for Death's ending is the Star's healing: after the change, the quiet rebuilding begins.

prescribedAct.value: Let one thing end today that has already finished, and do not try to revive it.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of release. Death's lesson is that the ending is not the opposite of life; it is the condition of the next life.

detailedReading: Death is the card of transformation and the ending that makes the next form possible, and its detailed features show how that transformation is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the skeleton, the white horse, and the rising sun mark it as the card of transformation. The numerical degree is thirteen — the number of transformation and the end of a cycle — and the posture is the skeleton riding upright on the horse, the king fallen beneath. The gesture is the carrying of the black banner with the white rose: the end marked by purity. The central object is the banner. The creature is the white horse, the creature of the apocalypse. The landscape is the world that is being left and the world that is being born: the two towers, the rising sun. There is no creature other than the horse, no tool other than the banner, no written word, no wound, and no binding: Death is not armed, not following a text, not suffering, and not bound. The inversion of the social order is present: the king is fallen, the order is inverted. The prescribed act follows from this: let one thing end today that has already finished, and do not try to revive it. The remedy is healing — the Star's quiet rebuilding — because the ending needs to be corrected by the capacity to heal.

name: Temperance
symbols: An angel pours water between two cups — the careful mixing of elements into something new.
One foot stands in a pool, the other on land — the conscious and unconscious held together.
A path winds toward the sun — the long, patient route of the work.
Irises grow beside her — faith, and the flower of the rainbow that follows the storm.

reading.upright: Temperance is the alchemy of balance: patience, the blending of opposites, and the slow work of making one thing out of two. Moderation and faithful process.
reading.reversed: Reversed, Temperance has tipped: excess, haste, or an incompatible mixing that cannot hold.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the angel, the cups, the pool, the irises)
elementalRegister.note: Temperance is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by water: the angel, the cups, the pool, and the irises mark it as the card of alchemical balance and the patient mixing of opposites.

numericalDegree.note: Fourteen is the number of the alchemical process, the point at which the opposites are blended into a new form. Temperance is the fourteenth point, the moment of balance.

courtFunction.note: Temperance is not a court card; it is the archetype of balance and alchemy.

figureType.value: A winged angel, human in form, pouring water between two cups
figureType.note: The angel is the figure of the alchemical process. It is human in form but divine in nature, marking the work as both human and cosmic.

posture.value: Standing with one foot in the pool and one on land
posture.note: The posture is one of balance between two worlds: the conscious (land) and the unconscious (water). The angel is the point at which the two are held together.

gesture.value: Pouring water from one cup to the other
gesture.note: The gesture is the gesture of alchemy: the careful mixing of elements into something new. The water is not spilled; it is transferred.

gaze.value: Looking at the cups, focused on the pouring
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of attention. The angel is watching the process, not the destination.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. Temperance is the card of the still point at which the mixing happens.

centralObject.value: The two cups and the water
centralObject.note: The cups are the vessels; the water is the substance. The central object is the act of transfer, the mixing itself.

heldObject.note: The cups are held, one in each hand. The holding is the holding of the two opposites, brought into relation.

creature.note: There is no creature. Temperance is a card of the angelic and the human, not of the animal.

tool.note: The tools are the vessels of the alchemical process. They are not weapons; they are instruments of transformation.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. Temperance's law is not written; it is enacted in the pouring.

landscape.value: A pool of water, a path, and irises
landscape.note: The landscape is the world of the alchemical process: the water, the path, and the flowers. It is a place of growth and transformation.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. Temperance is in the open, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.value: The pool's edge is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the line between the water and the land, the unconscious and the conscious. The angel stands on both.

celestialBody.note: The sun is the celestial body of the destination. It is the light toward which the path leads.

weather.note: The weather is fair. Temperance is not in a storm; the work is patient and calm.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the two cups, the two feet)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the two cups, the two feet, the two worlds. The symmetry is the symmetry of the alchemical balance.

repetitionCount.value: Two cups, two feet, two worlds
repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of polarity. The repetitions are the structural expression of the card's theme of balance.

verticalAxis.value: The angel above, the water below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the angelic to the watery. The angel is the point of connection.

horizontalAxis.value: The two cups held to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the transfer: the water moving from one cup to the other.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. Temperance is upright and balanced.

clothing.value: White robes
clothing.note: White is the colour of purity and balance. The robes mark the angel as a figure of the alchemical process.

nudity.note: The angel is fully clothed. The work is mediated by form and patience.

crown.note: There is no crown. The angel's authority is not social; it is the authority of the process.

wound.note: There is no wound. Temperance is not suffering; it is balancing.

binding.note: There are no chains. The angel is free to pour.

water.value: The pool and the poured water
water.note: Water is the dominant element of the card. It is the substance of the alchemical process, the unconscious, and the flow of life.

fire.note: There is no fire. Temperance's element is water and spirit, not fire.

vegetation.note: The irises are the flowers of faith and the rainbow. They mark the card as a card of hope and the promise of the new form.

stone.note: There is no stone. Temperance's world is fluid and soft, not hard and unyielding.

polarity.note: Temperance's remedy-pair is the Devil: she is balance, he is excess. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for Temperance's balance is the Devil's excess: sometimes the balance must be broken by the raw energy of desire.

prescribedAct.value: Blend two things today that you have kept separate, and see what new form emerges.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of alchemy. Temperance's lesson is that the new form is not arrived at by choosing one side; it is arrived at by mixing both.

detailedReading: Temperance is the card of alchemical balance and the patient mixing of opposites, and its detailed features show how that balance is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the angel, the cups, the pool, and the irises mark it as the card of alchemical balance. The numerical degree is fourteen — the number of the alchemical process — and the posture is standing with one foot in the pool and one on land. The gesture is the pouring of water from one cup to the other: the careful mixing of elements into something new. The central objects are the two cups and the water. The landscape is the pool, the path, and the irises. There is no creature, no written word, no wound, and no binding: Temperance is a card of the angelic and the human, not of the animal; its law is enacted, not written; it is not suffering; and it is free to pour. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the alchemical balance. The prescribed act follows from this: blend two things today that you have kept separate, and see what new form emerges. The remedy is excess — the Devil's raw energy — because the balance needs to be corrected by the capacity to break it.

name: The Devil
symbols: A horned, bat-winged figure presides — the shadow, the part of the self that binds.
Two figures are chained to his pedestal — but the chains hang loose around their necks.
An inverted pentagram above his head — spirit turned upside down, matter at the top.
A torch is held downward — the fire of the will misused, burning toward the ground.

reading.upright: The Devil is bondage — but bondage that is largely chosen. Materialism, addiction, a shadow that has been given more power than it has.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Devil is seen for what he is: the chains are recognised, and the work of release begins.

elementalRegister.value: Earth / Spirit (Major Arcana; the horned figure, the chains, the inverted pentagram)
elementalRegister.note: The Devil is a Major Arcana card, but his imagery is dominated by earth: the horned figure, the chains, and the inverted pentagram mark him as the card of bondage, materialism, and the shadow.

numericalDegree.note: Fifteen is the number of the shadow and the material world. The Devil is the fifteenth point, the moment at which the spirit is bound to matter.

courtFunction.note: The Devil is not a court card; he is the archetype of bondage and the shadow.

figureType.value: A horned, bat-winged human figure, with two chained humans
figureType.note: The Devil is a hybrid figure, part human and part animal. The two chained humans are the figures of the bound self.

posture.value: The Devil sits on a pedestal; the two humans stand, chained
posture.note: The posture of the Devil is one of authority; the posture of the humans is one of bondage. The contrast is the point of the card.

gesture.value: The Devil raises one hand; the other holds a downward torch
gesture.note: The raised hand is the gesture of power; the downward torch is the gesture of the fire that burns toward the ground. The gestures are the gestures of misused will.

gaze.value: The Devil looks forward; the humans look away or down
gaze.note: The gaze of the Devil is the gaze of domination; the gaze of the humans is the gaze of the bound.

movementDirection.value: Static (the Devil sits, the humans stand)
movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Devil is the card of the fixed state of bondage.

centralObject.value: The inverted pentagram and the chains
centralObject.note: The pentagram is the symbol of spirit turned upside down; the chains are the symbols of bondage. Both are the instruments of the shadow.

heldObject.note: The torch is held downward, the fire of the will misused. It is the fire that burns toward the ground rather than toward the sky.

creature.value: The Devil's horns and wings (animal features)
creature.note: The Devil's animal features are the marks of the shadow: the part of the self that is not fully human, not fully conscious.

tool.note: The tools are the instruments of bondage: the chains that bind and the torch that misdirects the fire.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Devil's law is not written; it is enacted in the chains.

landscape.value: A dark, cavernous space
landscape.note: The landscape is dark and enclosed. The Devil is not in the open world; he is in the cavern of the shadow.

architecture.note: The architecture is the pedestal on which the Devil sits. It is the seat of his authority.

threshold.note: The chains are the threshold between freedom and bondage. The humans are on the threshold, but they have not crossed it.

celestialBody.value: Absent (the inverted pentagram is the only celestial mark)
celestialBody.note: There is no celestial body. The inverted pentagram is the mark of the spirit turned away from the heavens.

weather.note: There is no weather. The Devil is in an interior space, the cavern of the shadow.

symmetry.value: Balanced and symmetrical
symmetry.note: The composition is symmetrical: the Devil in the centre, the two humans on either side. The symmetry is the symmetry of the bound state.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of the bound pair. The two humans and the two chains are the structural expression of the card's theme.

verticalAxis.value: The inverted pentagram above, the chains below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is inverted: the spirit is below, the matter is above. The Devil is the point of inversion.

horizontalAxis.value: The two humans on either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of bondage: the two humans are chained to the same pedestal.

inversion.value: Present (the inverted pentagram, the downward torch)
inversion.note: The inversion is the central feature of the card. The Devil is the card of the spirit turned upside down, the fire burning toward the ground.

clothing.value: The Devil is nude or partially clothed; the humans are nude
clothing.note: The nudity is the nudity of exposure, not of innocence. The humans are stripped of their defences.

nudity.value: Present (the humans are nude, the Devil is partially nude)
nudity.note: The nudity is the mark of vulnerability and exposure. The humans are exposed to the shadow.

crown.note: The Devil wears no crown, but the horns are the mark of his authority. It is an authority of the shadow, not of the light.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Devil is not suffering; he is binding.

binding.note: The chains are the central binding of the card. They are the bonds of the shadow, the addictions and attachments that hold the self.

water.note: There is no water. The Devil's element is earth and spirit, not water.

fire.note: The fire is the fire of the will, but it is held downward. It is the fire that burns toward the ground, not toward the sky.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Devil's world is barren and dark.

stone.note: Stone is present as the pedestal, the seat of the Devil's authority.

polarity.note: The Devil's remedy-pair is the Hierophant: he is instinct and the breaking of form, the Hierophant is tradition and institution. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Devil's excess is the Hierophant's tradition: sometimes the raw energy of desire needs to be corrected by the inherited form.

prescribedAct.value: Name one chain you are holding, and ask whether it is actually locked.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of awareness. The Devil's lesson is that the chains are often looser than they appear.

detailedReading: The Devil is the card of bondage and the shadow, and its detailed features show how that bondage is structured. Its elemental register is earth and spirit: the horned figure, the chains, and the inverted pentagram mark him as the card of bondage, materialism, and the shadow. The numerical degree is fifteen — the number of the shadow and the material world — and the posture is the Devil seated on a pedestal, the two humans standing, chained. The gesture is one of misused will: the raised hand, the downward torch. The central objects are the inverted pentagram and the chains. The creature is the Devil's own animal features, the horns and wings. The landscape is dark and enclosed, a cavern of the shadow. There is no creature other than the Devil himself, no written word, no wound, and the binding is the chains, the central feature of the card. The inversion is present in the pentagram and the torch: the spirit is turned upside down. The prescribed act follows from this: name one chain you are holding, and ask whether it is actually locked. The remedy is tradition — the Hierophant's inherited form — because the shadow needs to be corrected by the capacity to submit to a form.

name: The Tower
symbols: Lightning strikes the crown from the top of a tower — the false certainty that has been built up is not the truth.
Two figures fall headfirst — the fall is unavoidable, and it is total.
The tower stands on a jagged peak — the structure was already precarious, and everyone knew.
Flames pour from the windows — the destruction is also a revelation; the tower was never what it claimed.

reading.upright: The Tower is sudden, total disruption: a structure built on false certainty is torn down. Not punishment but revelation — the truth breaking through what could no longer stand.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Tower is delayed or resisted: a disaster held off, or an inner upheaval that has not yet broken the surface.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; lightning, flames, the tower)
elementalRegister.note: The Tower is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by fire: the lightning, the flames, and the tower mark it as the card of sudden disruption and revelation.

numericalDegree.note: Sixteen reduces to seven (1+6), linking it to the Chariot's drive and the tension of opposing forces; it is the degree at which a structure is tested.

courtFunction.note: The Tower is not a court card; it is the archetype of sudden change.

figureType.value: Two human figures falling headfirst from the tower
figureType.note: The humans are not the agents of the card; they are the ones caught in the collapse. The absence of a central protagonist means the event is structural, not personal.

posture.value: Falling headfirst, inverted
posture.note: The posture is the posture of being overturned by an external force. It is not chosen, unlike the Hanged Man's suspension.

gesture.value: Arms flailing or outstretched as they fall
gesture.note: The gesture is the gesture of the fall: there is no control, no holding, no direction.

gaze.value: Faces turned downward or away
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of the falling: they are looking at the ground that is coming, not at the sky.

movementDirection.note: Downward movement is the opposite of the deck's usual rightward/future orientation; it signals a reversal of expected progress.

centralObject.value: The tower, the lightning, and the falling crown
centralObject.note: The tower is the false certainty; the lightning is the revelation; the falling crown is the loss of authority.

heldObject.note: There is nothing held. The fall strips away everything that was held.

creature.note: There is no creature. The Tower is a card of human structures, not of instinct.

tool.value: Absent (the lightning is not a tool)
tool.note: There is no tool. The Tower is the card of the event that comes from outside, not from the will.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Tower's revelation is not written; it is enacted in the collapse.

landscape.value: A jagged peak with a tower on it
landscape.note: The landscape is the precarious ground on which the tower was built. The jagged peak is the instability that was always there.

architecture.note: The tower is the architecture of false certainty. Its height is both its pride and its vulnerability.

threshold.value: The tower's top is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the point at which the tower meets the lightning. It is the point of revelation.

celestialBody.note: The lightning is the celestial force that breaks the tower. It is the revelation that comes from above.

weather.note: The weather is the visible agent of disruption. The storm is the atmosphere of the revelation.

symmetry.value: Asymmetrical (the tower is off-centre, the figures fall)
symmetry.note: The composition is asymmetrical. The Tower is a card of disruption, not of balance.

repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of the falling pair. The two figures are the human cost of the collapse.

verticalAxis.value: The tower rises, the figures fall
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis is the axis of the fall: the tower rises, the figures fall from it.

horizontalAxis.value: The lightning strikes from the side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the strike: the lightning comes from the side, breaking the vertical structure.

inversion.value: Present (the figures fall headfirst, the crown is struck off)
inversion.note: The inversion is the inversion of the expected order: the figures fall headfirst, the crown is struck from the top.

clothing.value: The figures are in simple clothing
clothing.note: The clothing is simple. The Tower strips away the markers of status.

nudity.note: The figures are clothed, but their clothing does not protect them. The fall is total.

crown.value: A crown struck from the tower
crown.note: The crown is the mark of authority, and it is struck away. The Tower is the card that shows the limits of all authority.

wound.value: Absent (the figures are falling, not wounded)
wound.note: There is no wound, but the fall is the wound. The Tower is the card of the injury that is also a revelation.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Tower is the unbinding, the breaking of the structure.

water.note: There is no water. The Tower's element is fire, not water.

fire.value: The lightning and the flames from the windows
fire.note: Fire is the dominant element of the card. It is the fire of destruction that is also purification.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Tower is a card of the barren ground of the collapse.

stone.value: The tower and the jagged peak
stone.note: Stone is the material of the tower and the peak. The Tower is built on stone, but the stone itself is precarious.

polarity.note: The Tower's remedy-pair is the Star: he is the collapse, she is the healing. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Tower's collapse is the Star's quiet rebuilding: after the fall, the slow healing begins.

prescribedAct.value: Do not rescue what is falling; wait for the ground to clear, and look for the small, clean thing that remains.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of restraint. The Tower's lesson is that not everything that falls needs to be saved.

detailedReading: The Tower is the card of sudden disruption and revelation, and its detailed features show how that disruption is structured. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the lightning, the flames, and the tower mark it as the card of sudden disruption. The numerical degree is sixteen — the degree at which a structure is tested — and the posture is the posture of the fall: the two figures falling headfirst, inverted. The central objects are the tower, the lightning, and the falling crown. The landscape is the jagged peak, the precarious ground on which the tower was built. There is no creature, no tool, no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Tower is a card of human structures, not of instinct; the event comes from outside, not from the will; the revelation is enacted, not written; the fall is the wound; and there are no chains, only the unbinding. The inversion of the figures and the crown is the central feature of the card. The prescribed act follows from this: do not rescue what is falling; wait for the ground to clear, and look for the small, clean thing that remains. The remedy is healing — the Star's quiet rebuilding — because the collapse needs to be corrected by the capacity to heal.

name: The Star
symbols: A nude figure pours water onto the land and into a pool — unselfconscious giving, in both directions.
One foot rests in the pool, the other on land — the two worlds, kept together.
Eight stars shine above — regeneration, the number of return after the storm.
An ibis on a nearby tree — wisdom, watching from its own place.

reading.upright: The Star is the calm after the Tower: hope, healing, and the quiet return of inspiration. It favours faith in the process and trust in what is being rebuilt.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Star is dimmed: hope lost, faith in the process exhausted, and a tiredness that cannot yet see renewal.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the pool, the stars, the nude figure)
elementalRegister.note: The Star is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by water: the pool, the stars, and the nude figure mark it as the card of hope, healing, and the renewal that follows the storm.

numericalDegree.note: Seventeen reduces to eight (1+7), linking it to Strength's balance and regeneration. It is the degree at which the healing begins.

courtFunction.note: The Star is not a court card; it is the archetype of hope and renewal.

figureType.value: A nude human woman, kneeling by a pool
figureType.note: She is human and nude, kneeling by the water. Her nudity is the nudity of innocence and exposure, not of shame.

posture.value: Kneeling, one foot in the pool, one on land
posture.note: The posture is one of balance between two worlds: the conscious (land) and the unconscious (water). The kneeling is the posture of humility and reception.

gesture.value: Pouring water from two vessels, one onto the land, one into the pool
gesture.note: The gesture is one of unselfconscious giving, in both directions. The water is given to the earth and to the pool; it is not hoarded.

gaze.value: Looking down at the water or at the pouring
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of attention. The figure is watching the water, not the stars.

movementDirection.note: There is no movement. The Star is the card of the still point of healing.

centralObject.value: The two vessels and the water
centralObject.note: The vessels are the instruments of giving; the water is the substance of healing. The central object is the act of pouring.

heldObject.note: The vessels are held, one in each hand. The holding is the holding of the two worlds, brought into relation.

creature.value: An ibis on a nearby tree
creature.note: The ibis is the bird of wisdom, watching from its own place. It is the presence of the sacred in the natural world.

tool.note: The tools are the vessels of giving. They are not weapons; they are instruments of healing.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Star's law is not written; it is enacted in the pouring.

landscape.value: A pool of water, a tree, and a landscape
landscape.note: The landscape is the world of healing: the water, the tree, and the open ground. It is a place of renewal.

architecture.note: There is no architecture. The Star is in the open, not in a city or a temple.

threshold.value: The pool's edge is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the line between the water and the land, the unconscious and the conscious. The figure stands on both.

celestialBody.value: Eight stars in the sky, one large and seven small
celestialBody.note: The stars are the celestial bodies of hope and regeneration. The large star is the point of guidance; the seven small stars are the return of the light.

weather.note: The weather is fair. The Star is the calm after the Tower; the storm has passed.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the two vessels, the two feet)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the two vessels, the two feet, the two worlds. The symmetry is the symmetry of the healing.

repetitionCount.note: The number eight is the number of regeneration. The eight stars are the structural expression of the card's theme.

verticalAxis.value: The stars above, the pool below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the stars) to the watery (the pool). The figure is the point of connection.

horizontalAxis.value: The two vessels held to either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the pouring: the water moving from one vessel to the land, from the other to the pool.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Star is upright and balanced.

clothing.value: Absent (the figure is nude)
clothing.note: The figure is nude. Her nudity is the nudity of innocence and exposure, not of shame.

nudity.note: The nudity is the central feature of the card. It is the mark of the unselfconscious giving, the absence of defence.

crown.note: There is no crown. The Star's authority is not social; it is the authority of hope.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Star is the card of healing, not of injury.

binding.note: There are no chains. The figure is free to pour.

water.value: The pool and the poured water
water.note: Water is the dominant element of the card. It is the substance of healing, the unconscious, and the flow of life.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Star's element is water and spirit, not fire.

vegetation.note: The tree is the living world, the place of the ibis. It marks the card as a card of life and growth.

stone.note: There is no stone. The Star's world is fluid and soft, not hard and unyielding.

polarity.note: The Star's remedy-pair is the Tower: she is healing, he is collapse. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Star's healing is the Tower's collapse: sometimes the healing must be preceded by the breaking of what cannot stand.

prescribedAct.value: Give something away today without expecting anything in return, and let the giving be the healing.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of unselfconscious giving. The Star's lesson is that healing is not seized; it is poured out.

detailedReading: The Star is the card of hope and renewal, and its detailed features show how that renewal is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the pool, the stars, and the nude figure mark it as the card of hope, healing, and the renewal that follows the storm. The numerical degree is seventeen — the degree at which the healing begins — and the posture is kneeling, one foot in the pool, one on land. The gesture is one of unselfconscious giving, in both directions: the water is poured onto the land and into the pool. The central objects are the two vessels and the water. The creature is the ibis, the bird of wisdom. The landscape is the pool, the tree, and the open ground, and the stars are the celestial bodies of hope. There is no architecture, no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Star is in the open, its law is enacted, it is not suffering, and the figure is free to pour. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the healing. The prescribed act follows from this: give something away today without expecting anything in return, and let the giving be the healing. The remedy is collapse — the Tower's breaking — because the healing needs to be corrected by the recognition that some things must fall before they can be rebuilt.

name: The Moon
symbols: A moon with a face shines in a deep sky — light that reflects rather than reveals, casting the world in doubt.
A dog and a wolf howl at it — the tame and the wild instinct, both made uneasy by the night.
A crayfish crawls out of a pool — the deep, unrecognised material rising to the surface.
A path leads between two towers — the way forward is narrow, and only partly visible.

reading.upright: The Moon is ambiguity and illusion: what is seen is not clearly what is there. It favours intuition over certainty, and patience while the unclear clarifies.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Moon's fog is lifting — a confusion begins to resolve, a hidden thing comes into view.

elementalRegister.value: Water / Spirit (Major Arcana; the moon, the pool, the crayfish)
elementalRegister.note: The Moon is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by water: the moon, the pool, and the crayfish mark it as the card of ambiguity, illusion, and the deep unconscious.

numericalDegree.note: Eighteen reduces to nine (1+8), linking it to the Hermit's solitude and the threshold of a new cycle. It is the degree at which the unconscious surfaces.

courtFunction.note: The Moon is not a court card; it is the archetype of ambiguity and the unconscious.

figureType.value: A moon with a face, a dog, a wolf, and a crayfish
figureType.note: The figures are not human. They are the cosmic and animal forces of the night: the moon, the dog, the wolf, and the crayfish.

posture.value: The dog and wolf stand and howl; the crayfish crawls out of the pool
posture.note: The postures are the postures of unease and emergence: the howling animals, the rising crayfish.

gesture.value: The animals howl at the moon; the crayfish emerges
gesture.note: The gestures are the gestures of response: the animals respond to the moon, the crayfish responds to the pull of the deep.

gaze.value: The animals look up at the moon; the moon looks down
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of the night: the animals look up, the moon looks down. The exchange is the exchange of the conscious and the unconscious.

movementDirection.value: The crayfish emerges from the pool; the path leads between two towers
movementDirection.note: The movement is the movement of emergence and passage: the crayfish rises, the path leads forward.

centralObject.value: The moon
centralObject.note: The moon is the central object, the light that reflects rather than reveals. It is the source of the ambiguity.

heldObject.note: There is nothing held. The Moon is a card of reception and response, not of holding.

creature.value: A dog, a wolf, and a crayfish
creature.note: The dog is the tame instinct, the wolf the wild instinct, the crayfish the deep unconscious. All three are the creatures of the night.

tool.note: There is no tool. The Moon is a card of the unconscious, not of the will.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Moon's law is not written; it is felt.

landscape.value: A pool, a path between two towers, and a deep sky
landscape.note: The landscape is the night world: the pool of the unconscious, the path of the conscious, and the sky of the cosmic.

architecture.note: The two towers are the architecture of the threshold. They mark the passage between the known and the unknown.

threshold.value: The path between the two towers is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the narrow path between the two towers. It is the way forward, but it is only partly visible.

celestialBody.note: The moon is the celestial body of the night. It is the light that reflects rather than reveals, casting the world in doubt.

weather.note: The weather is the night. The Moon is the card of the dark, the ambiguous, the not-yet-clear.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the two towers, the two animals)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the two towers, the two animals. The symmetry is the symmetry of the night world.

repetitionCount.value: Two towers, two animals (dog and wolf)
repetitionCount.note: The number two is the number of polarity. The repetitions are the structural expression of the card's theme of the paired opposites.

verticalAxis.value: The moon above, the pool below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the moon) to the watery (the pool). The crayfish is the point of emergence.

horizontalAxis.value: The two towers on either side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the passage: the two towers mark the way through.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Moon is upright, though its light is indirect.

clothing.value: Absent (the creatures are unclothed)
clothing.note: The creatures are unclothed. The Moon is a card of the natural and the unconscious, not of culture.

nudity.value: Absent (the creatures are animals, not human)
nudity.note: There is no human nudity. The Moon is a card of the animal and the cosmic, not of the human.

crown.note: There is no crown. The Moon is not a card of social authority.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Moon is not a card of suffering; it is a card of ambiguity.

binding.note: There are no chains. The Moon is a card of the free, if uncertain, night.

water.note: The pool is the water of the unconscious. It is the deep from which the crayfish emerges.

fire.note: There is no fire. The Moon's element is water and spirit, not fire.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. The Moon is a card of the barren night.

stone.note: Stone is present as the two towers, the architecture of the threshold.

polarity.note: The Moon's remedy-pair is the Sun: she is ambiguity, he is clarity. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Moon's ambiguity is the Sun's clarity: sometimes the fog must be burned off by the direct light.

prescribedAct.value: Do not decide today; let the unclear stay unclear, and watch what emerges from the pool.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of patience. The Moon's lesson is that not all ambiguity is a problem to be solved; some of it is a depth to be entered.

detailedReading: The Moon is the card of ambiguity and the unconscious, and its detailed features show how that ambiguity is structured. Its elemental register is water and spirit: the moon, the pool, and the crayfish mark it as the card of ambiguity, illusion, and the deep unconscious. The numerical degree is eighteen — the degree at which the unconscious surfaces — and the posture is the posture of the night: the dog and wolf howling, the crayfish emerging. The central object is the moon, the light that reflects rather than reveals. The creatures are the dog (the tame instinct), the wolf (the wild instinct), and the crayfish (the deep unconscious). The landscape is the pool, the path between two towers, and the deep sky. There is no tool, no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Moon is a card of the unconscious, not of the will; its law is felt, not written; it is not suffering; and it is free. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the night world. The prescribed act follows from this: do not decide today; let the unclear stay unclear, and watch what emerges from the pool. The remedy is clarity — the Sun's direct light — because the ambiguity needs to be corrected by the capacity to see.

name: The Sun
symbols: A child rides a white horse — innocent confidence, fully at ease in the light.
Sunflowers turn openly toward the sun — growth that is not ashamed of its own wanting.
A red banner flies behind the child — the vital energy of a life that is being lived.
A walled garden surrounds him — safety, but a safety with open sky above it.

reading.upright: The Sun is the uncomplicated good: joy, clarity, vitality, and the sense that things are, on the whole, going well. Success that can be felt as well as known.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the Sun is behind a cloud: joy available but not quite reached, pessimism colouring what is actually fine.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; the sun, the sunflowers, the child)
elementalRegister.note: The Sun is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by fire: the sun, the sunflowers, and the child mark it as the card of joy, vitality, and clear success.

numericalDegree.note: Nineteen reduces to ten (1+9), linking it to the Wheel's completion and the return to the beginning. It is the degree at which the light is full.

courtFunction.note: The Sun is not a court card; it is the archetype of joy and clarity.

figureType.value: A nude child on a white horse
figureType.note: The child is the figure of innocence and confidence. The horse is the creature of vitality, and the child rides it without fear.

posture.value: The child rides upright on the horse, arms open
posture.note: The posture is one of open confidence. The child is not clinging to the horse; he is riding it with ease.

gesture.value: Arms open, one hand holding a banner
gesture.note: The gesture is one of openness and display. The banner is held aloft, the arms are open to the light.

gaze.value: Facing forward or slightly upward, toward the sun
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of confidence. The child is looking at the light, not away from it.

movementDirection.note: The movement is forward, the movement of vitality. The Sun is the card of progress and success.

centralObject.value: The sun and the red banner
centralObject.note: The sun is the source of the light; the banner is the mark of the child's vitality. Both are the symbols of the card's joy.

heldObject.note: The banner is held aloft. It is the standard of the life that is being lived.

creature.note: The horse is the creature of vitality and movement. It is white, the colour of purity, and it carries the child forward.

tool.note: The tool is the banner, not a sword. The Sun is a card of celebration, not of conflict.

writtenWord.note: There is no text. The Sun's law is not written; it is felt in the light.

landscape.value: A walled garden with sunflowers
landscape.note: The landscape is the garden, the place of cultivated growth. It is safe and open to the sky.

architecture.note: The wall is the architecture of safety. But the sky above is open, and the sun is not enclosed.

threshold.value: The garden wall is the threshold
threshold.note: The threshold is the wall of the garden. The child is within it, but the sun is above it.

celestialBody.note: The sun is the celestial body of clarity and vitality. It is the source of the card's joy.

weather.note: The weather is fair. The Sun is the card of the clear day.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the child in the centre, the sun above, the sunflowers to the side)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced. The symmetry is the symmetry of the full light.

repetitionCount.value: Four sunflowers (or a field of them)
repetitionCount.note: The sunflowers are the repetitions of the card. They are the flowers that turn toward the light.

verticalAxis.value: The sun above, the child below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the sun) to the earthly (the child). The child is the point of reception.

horizontalAxis.value: The sunflowers and the garden to the side
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of growth: the sunflowers turn toward the sun.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. The Sun is upright and clear.

clothing.value: The child is nude; the banner is red
clothing.note: The child is nude, the nudity of innocence and confidence. The red banner is the colour of vitality.

nudity.note: The nudity is the nudity of innocence, not of shame. The child is fully at ease in the light.

crown.value: Absent (the child wears a wreath of flowers)
crown.note: There is no crown, but the wreath of flowers is the mark of the child's natural joy.

wound.note: There is no wound. The Sun is not a card of suffering; it is a card of joy.

binding.note: There are no chains. The child is free.

water.note: There is no water. The Sun's element is fire and spirit, not water.

fire.note: Fire is the dominant element of the card. It is the fire of life, not of destruction.

vegetation.note: The vegetation is the sunflowers, the flowers that turn toward the light. They mark the card as a card of growth and joy.

stone.note: Stone is present as the garden wall, the architecture of safety.

polarity.note: The Sun's remedy-pair is the Moon: he is clarity, she is ambiguity. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for the Sun's clarity is the Moon's ambiguity: sometimes the clear light must be corrected by the recognition that not everything is simple.

prescribedAct.value: Let yourself be seen today in your joy, without apology or explanation.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of openness. The Sun's lesson is that joy is not to be hidden; it is to be lived in the open.

detailedReading: The Sun is the card of joy and clarity, and its detailed features show how that joy is structured. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the sun, the sunflowers, and the child mark it as the card of joy, vitality, and clear success. The numerical degree is nineteen — the degree at which the light is full — and the posture is the child riding upright on the white horse, arms open. The gesture is one of openness and display: the banner held aloft, the arms open to the light. The central objects are the sun and the red banner. The creature is the white horse, the creature of vitality. The landscape is the walled garden with sunflowers, and the sun is the celestial body of clarity. There is no written word, no wound, and no binding: the Sun's law is felt, not written; it is not suffering; and the child is free. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the full light. The prescribed act follows from this: let yourself be seen today in your joy, without apology or explanation. The remedy is ambiguity — the Moon's depth — because the clarity needs to be corrected by the recognition that not everything is simple.

name: Judgement
symbols: An angel blows a trumpet — the call that cannot be unheard, arriving from beyond the self.
Figures rise from coffins with arms lifted — resurrection, the answering of the call.
A banner bears a cross — the union of above and below, spirit entering the world.
Mountains recede behind — the past, present but no longer in front.

reading.upright: Judgement is the awakening: the call that summons one to account and to rise. Reckoning, forgiveness, and the willingness to answer what has been heard.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the call is refused — self-doubt, harsh judgment of the self, or the coffin lid kept closed.

elementalRegister.value: Fire / Spirit (Major Arcana; the angel, the trumpet, the rising figures)
elementalRegister.note: Judgement is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by fire: the angel, the trumpet, and the rising figures mark it as the card of awakening, reckoning, and the call to rise.

numericalDegree.note: Twenty reduces to two (2+0), linking it to the High Priestess's polarity and the Lovers' choice. It is the degree at which the call is heard.

courtFunction.note: Judgement is not a court card; it is the archetype of awakening and reckoning.

figureType.value: An angel, and human figures rising from coffins
figureType.note: The angel is the figure of the call; the humans are the figures of the response. The card is the meeting of the two.

posture.value: The angel stands and blows the trumpet; the figures rise with arms lifted
posture.note: The postures are the postures of call and response: the angel standing, the figures rising.

gesture.value: The angel blows the trumpet; the figures lift their arms
gesture.note: The gestures are the gestures of awakening: the trumpet is the call, the lifted arms are the answer.

gaze.value: The angel looks forward; the figures look up
gaze.note: The gaze is the gaze of the call: the angel looks forward, the figures look up toward the sound.

movementDirection.note: The movement is upward, the movement of resurrection. Judgement is the card of rising.

centralObject.value: The trumpet and the cross on the banner
centralObject.note: The trumpet is the instrument of the call; the cross is the symbol of the union of above and below.

heldObject.note: The trumpet is held to the mouth; the banner is held aloft. Both are the instruments of the call.

creature.note: There is no creature. Judgement is a card of the angelic and the human, not of the animal.

tool.note: The tools are the instruments of the call: the trumpet that sounds and the banner that announces.

writtenWord.value: Absent (the cross is the only mark)
writtenWord.note: There is no text. The call is sounded, not written.

landscape.value: A landscape with mountains in the background
landscape.note: The landscape is the world that is being left behind. The mountains are the past, present but no longer in front.

architecture.value: Absent (the coffins are the only structures)
architecture.note: There is no architecture. Judgement is in the open, at the threshold of the resurrection.

threshold.note: The coffins are the threshold between death and life. The figures are rising from them.

celestialBody.note: The angel is the celestial presence that sounds the call. It is the mark of the divine initiative.

weather.note: The weather is fair. Judgement is the card of the clear day of reckoning.

symmetry.value: Balanced (the angel above, the figures below)
symmetry.note: The composition is balanced: the angel above, the figures below. The symmetry is the symmetry of the call and response.

repetitionCount.note: The number of the figures is the number of those who answer the call. Judgement is a collective card, not a solitary one.

verticalAxis.value: The angel above, the figures below
verticalAxis.note: The vertical axis connects the celestial (the angel) to the earthly (the figures). The call comes from above, the response from below.

horizontalAxis.value: The figures spread across the ground
horizontalAxis.note: The horizontal axis is the axis of the community: the figures are rising together.

inversion.note: There is no inversion. Judgement is upright and clear.

clothing.value: The angel is robed; the figures are nude or lightly clothed
clothing.note: The angel is robed, the figures are exposed. The nudity of the figures is the nudity of the resurrection, the stripping away of the old life.

nudity.value: Present (the figures are nude or lightly clothed)
nudity.note: The nudity is the nudity of rebirth. The figures are rising naked, stripped of the old life.

crown.note: There is no crown. Judgement is not a card of social authority.

wound.note: There is no wound. Judgement is not a card of suffering; it is a card of awakening.

binding.note: There are no chains. The figures are rising free.

water.note: There is no water. Judgement's element is fire and spirit, not water.

fire.value: The angel's trumpet (the fire of the call)
fire.note: The fire is the fire of the call, the heat of the awakening.

vegetation.note: There is no vegetation. Judgement is a card of the bare ground of the resurrection.

stone.note: Stone is present as the coffins, the structures of the old life.

polarity.note: Judgement's remedy-pair is the Fool: he is the beginning, Judgement is the awakening. Each is the corrective to the other's excess.

remedy.note: The remedy for Judgement's reckoning is the Fool's beginning: sometimes the awakening must be followed by a new step into the unknown.

prescribedAct.value: Answer one call today that you have been pretending not to hear.
prescribedAct.note: The act is the discipline of response. Judgement's lesson is that the call is not a punishment; it is an invitation to rise.

detailedReading: Judgement is the card of awakening and reckoning, and its detailed features show how that awakening is structured. Its elemental register is fire and spirit: the angel, the trumpet, and the rising figures mark it as the card of awakening, reckoning, and the call to rise. The numerical degree is twenty — the degree at which the call is heard — and the posture is the posture of call and response: the angel standing, the figures rising with arms lifted. The central objects are the trumpet and the cross on the banner. The landscape is the world that is being left behind, with mountains in the background. There is no creature, no tool other than the trumpet and banner, no written word, no wound, and no binding: Judgement is a card of the angelic and the human, not of the animal; its tools are the instruments of the call; its law is sounded, not written; it is not suffering; and the figures are rising free. The symmetry of the composition is the symmetry of the call and response. The prescribed act follows from this: answer one call today that you have been pretending not to hear. The remedy is beginning — the Fool's new step — because the awakening needs to be corrected by the capacity to begin again.

name: The World
symbols: A figure stands inside a great wreath — the whole cycle, embraced rather than escaped.
Two wands are held in her hands — will and matter, finally balanced.
Four creatures hold the corners — the four elements, now in their places.
A scarf or veil moves around her — the completion is alive, still in motion.

reading.upright: The World is the completion of a cycle: wholeness, fulfilment, and the arrival at a place from which the next beginning can be seen.
reading.reversed: Reversed, the World is near-completion: the last step delayed, or the cycle finished in form but not yet in meaning.

elementalRegister.value: Earth / Spirit (Major Arcana; the wreath, the four creatures, the dancing figure)
elementalRegister.note: The World is a Major Arcana card, and its imagery is dominated by earth: the wreath, the four creatures, and the dancing figure mark it as the card of completion and wholeness.
